Title: Endogenous Location and Pricing Policy: Mixed Strategies Make Uniform Pricing Commitment Successful
Does regulation bite at gateways? Evidence from MiCA and stablecoins
Abstract: Gateways are trading venues where regulation can change the assets investors can trade. We study this margin using MiCA-EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation-which led several exchanges to delist USDT pairs for European Economic Area users, while USDC obtained MiCA authorization. First, aggregate market shares and trading volumes barely move. Second, comparing Regulated-facing exchanges with globally oriented exchanges where MiCA is less likely to bind, we show that the cross-section shifts toward USDC-USDC share rises by 0.82 and relative trading volume by 0.54 pre-event standard deviations. Both reflect USDT trading contracting where it is delisted.

Title: Trade Policy Uncertainty and Stock Market Tail Risk
Authors: Tobias Adrian, Andrea Deghi, Mahvash S. Qureshi, Mustafa Yasin Yenice

Title: Inductive inference for restricted stochastic dominance
The entrepreneurship U-shape: Pattern or path?
Abstract: A familiar U-shape links early-stage entrepreneurship to income per capita and is often read as a development path. I test that reading by asking whether the curve turns inside observed support, where it is located, and whether it survives within countries. The pooled quadratic opens upward but does not turn inside observed support. The in-support U-shape appears only among high-income economies. Within that group, country fixed effects detect no significant curvature, and the Mundlak point estimates show positive between-country but near-zero within-country curvature. The evidence is stronger for a cross-sectional pattern among rich economies than for a common within-country path.

Title: Beyond GDP tournaments: Cadre evaluation reform and sectoral credit allocation
The effects of allocation authority on cooperation and free-riding in sequential public goods games
Inference for partially functional coefficient models with endogeneity
Authors: Yujian Chen, Jingrong Li, Ji-Liang Shiu, Zizhong Yan

Title: The 2025 U.S. tariffs on China and trade diversion to the EU
Authors: Patrick Schulte, Almira Enders, Andreas Esser, Felix Strobel
Abstract: We study whether bilateral trade barriers trigger trade diversion to third markets, using the 2025 increase in U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods and focusing on the European Union as an alternative destination. At the HS6 level, we construct a novel diversion-potential measure that combines realized U.S. tariff increases with product-level trade elasticities to predict the decline in Chinese exports to the United States. Trade diversion effects are limited to highly exposed products. Only products in the top decile of diversion potential experience a rise in export quantities to the EU. Unit values do not respond significantly.

Title: Where machines improve: Automation direction, task boundaries, and the skill premium
Abstract: Automation technologies can affect wage inequality differently even when they automate the same measure of tasks. This paper studies a task-assignment model in which capital performs an endogenous interior interval of tasks. A uniform rise in machine productivity expands that interval from both sides. A rightward shift in the location of peak machine productivity moves both boundaries to the right and lowers the skill premium, while automated width may expand, contract, or remain locally unchanged. A closed-form boundary formula explains why the location of machine improvements matters separately from automated extent.

Title: The price of hope: Reference-group mobility and the subjective value of income
Abstract: We examine whether upward mobility within a person’s reference group changes the subjective value of own and reference income. Standard relative-income models interpret higher peer income mainly as status loss. We argue that this view is incomplete. In mobile reference groups, higher peer income may also signal attainable opportunities, consistent with a “tunnel effect”; at the same time, mobility can raise aspirations and reduce satisfaction with one’s own income, creating what we call the “price of hope”. Using the Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP) for 2000–2020, we combine individual fixed effects with leave-one-out reference income and leave-one-out reference-group-year measures of realised upward income dynamics. Among individuals below their reference income, the negative association between reference income and life satisfaction is strong in low-mobility environments but largely attenuated when mobility is high. The own-income gradient is also smaller in high-mobility environments. These patterns are weaker among individuals at or above their reference income and robust across alternative mobility measures, reference-group definitions, median reference income, and controls for within-group inequality. Mobility, therefore, changes the meaning of income: it makes richer peers less costly as a status benchmark, but lowers the subjective return to current own income by shifting aspirations upward.

Title: Harness the power law: Robust estimation of tail index and threshold
Authors: Kailin Ding, Zhenyu Cui, Qian Pan, Lingjiong Zhu
Abstract: Accurate tail index estimation is critical for measuring extreme risk in economic and financial systems. We propose a closed-form estimator, the Method of Truncated Moments (MTM), based on matching empirical and theoretical truncated moments. Unlike classical approaches, our method jointly determines the tail index and optimal tail region threshold, which reduces sensitivity to tuning parameters. MTM is asymptotically valid for regularly varying tails and offers an accuracy superior to modern benchmarks. It performs robustly in small samples and remains stable even when convergence to the Pareto limit is slow.

Title: When trust attracts fraud: AI and trust arbitrage
Abstract: Trust can attract fraud when it delays verification. We develop a two-market signaling model in which generative AI lowers fabrication, verification, and targeting costs. When fabrication becomes profitable before verification, claim credibility first falls and later recovers. Across markets, higher prior quality can delay verification, creating an interval in which only the lower-quality market checks. If targeting becomes profitable in this interval, deceptive sellers enter the higher-quality but less vigilant market, and their entry can initially reverse its reliability advantage. The inflow also triggers verification and deters further entry. We call this self-limiting mechanism trust arbitrage. In the age of generative AI, trust can thus create an endogenous but temporary protection gap that redirects deception across markets.

Title: The macroeconomic effects of purely forward-looking uncertainty shocks: Evidence from the euro area
Abstract: If the underlying data-generating process operates at a higher frequency than observed data, timing and dynamic restrictions in structural vector autoregressions (SVARs) may be misspecified. Building on Berger et al. (2020), I propose an alternative identification scheme that jointly relaxes the zero-impact restriction on realized volatility and the zero-lag restrictions on macroeconomic variables in the volatility block, estimated with a richer twelve-lag specification. Applied to euro area data, the identified shocks depress real activity gradually and with a delay, unlike the macro-neutral U.S. evidence, though they account for only a modest share of real fluctuations.

Title: Weaponized reputation: Experimental evidence on the misuse of coordinated punishments
Abstract: This paper experimentally studies how coordinated punishment can be misused. In a repeated trust game with public reputation, we compare a silent commitment treatment, where Agents privately choose a review threshold (the minimum payment required for a positive review), with a public commitment treatment, where the review threshold is observable before Principals choose payments. Public commitment significantly reduces cooperation: effort and payments fall relative to silent commitment. Public commitment also turns posted review thresholds into more enforceable demands: Principals are substantially more likely to meet visible thresholds. Successful zero-effort extraction, in which an Agent exerts no effort but sets a positive review threshold met by the Principal’s payment, is significantly more frequent under public commitment. Coordinated punishments can therefore discipline misconduct, but may also create tools for extortion.

Title: A rational bubble model with momentum
Geopolitical risk and fiscal financing capacity in E7 economies: does institutional quality matter?
Authors: Umar Farooq, Mosab I. Tabash, Abdulrahman Alomair, Abdulateif A. Almulhim
Abstract: This study examines whether geopolitical risk (GPR) affects tax revenue mobilization (TXR) in E7 economies and whether institutional quality (INQ) helps mitigate this effect. Using annual data for China, India, Brazil, Russia, Mexico, Indonesia, and Türkiye over 1985–2024, the study employs the Cross-Sectionally Augmented Autoregressive Distributed Lag (CS-ARDL) estimator, with Fully Modified Ordinary Least Squares (FMOLS) used for robustness. The results indicate that geopolitical risk significantly reduces tax revenue mobilization, while stronger institutional quality improves revenue performance. Moreover, the interaction between GPR and INQ is positive and significant, confirming that institutional quality weakens the adverse effect of geopolitical risk on tax revenue. The findings highlight the importance of institutional capacity in strengthening fiscal resilience and sustaining government financing capacity during periods of geopolitical uncertainty.

Title: The exchange rate puzzle and the systematic component of monetary policy: Evidence from Mexico
Authors: Jesús Eduardo López-Mares, Rogelio Varela-Llamas, Juan Manuel Ocegueda-Hernández
Abstract: This paper revisits the exchange rate puzzle following contractionary monetary policy shocks in a small open economy. Using a Bayesian SVAR for Mexico, we compare three cumulative identification schemes: pure sign restrictions on impulse response functions (IRFs), a closed-economy Taylor-type rule with contemporaneous sign and zero restrictions, and an exchange-rate-augmented rule. Neither pure sign restrictions nor the closed-economy rule yields a precisely estimated overshooting pattern—only the augmented rule does. Robust to alternative specifications, these results suggest that omitting the exchange rate from the systematic component of monetary policy may hinder shock identification in small open economies.

Title: The difficulty of telling signal from noise when noise lingers
Abstract: How many observations does it take to detect a fixed signal when the noise has long memory? For a sample-mean detector applied to a constant signal buried in fractionally integrated noise of order (Formula presented), I give a closed-form expression for the sample size required to reach a target power at a fixed size: (Formula presented). The exponent (Formula presented) is the whole story: the required sample size is a power function of detection difficulty whose exponent diverges as (Formula presented). A doubling of detection difficulty that costs four times the data under independence costs 210 times the data at (Formula presented). A Monte Carlo confirms the formula delivers the target power and size.

Title: How many sign restrictions are needed? A sharp lower bound for identifying multiple shocks in SVARs
Abstract: This paper derives the exact minimum number of impact sign restrictions required to identify m shocks in a structural vector autoregression under a natural pairwise separation condition. The answer is (Formula presented). The proof follows from deriving a sharp lower bound using a Kraft-type inequality and then constructing an admissible restriction matrix that attains the bound. Our result reveals a significant sparsity gain: while traditional recursive orderings require (Formula presented) restrictions, sign-based separation requires only (Formula presented), providing a transparent benchmark for designing sparse identifying schemes in large SVARs.

Title: Fiscal decentralization and the FDI–growth nexus
Abstract: This paper contributes to the recent literature on the FDI–growth nexus by investigating whether fiscal decentralization moderates the growth effects of foreign direct investment (FDI). Using a panel of 69 countries over 1996–2020 with fixed-effects and system-GMM estimations, we show that while FDI generally promotes economic growth, its positive effect is significantly attenuated in countries with higher levels of fiscal decentralization, on both the revenue and expenditure sides. We further identify infrastructure quality as a transmission channel through which expenditure decentralization dampens the FDI–growth nexus, suggesting a reduced capacity to finance national public goods in highly decentralized settings. These findings highlight the importance of intergovernmental coordination in preserving the growth effectiveness of foreign investment, and open new avenues for research on the institutional determinants of the FDI–growth nexus.

Title: Cryptocurrency denomination and NFT pricing
Authors: Jaehyeong Park, Euro Bae, Daegon Cho, Donghoon Kim
Abstract: Using transaction data from OpenSea, we examine how cryptocurrency price fluctuations affect NFT returns and whether these dynamics depend on denomination of cryptocurrency, across sequential stages: price setting (purchase-to-list) and price taking (list-to-sale). Panel regressions on 46,671 repeated NFT sales reveal that sellers anchor listing prices to acquisition prices, generating asymmetric mark-ups during ETH appreciation and mark-downs during ETH depreciation. Buyers exhibit similar anchor sale prices to listing prices. Stablecoin-denominated acquisition prices partially mitigate these distortions. These findings extend the denomination and anchoring literature to highly volatile, multi-currency marketplaces.

Title: The reverse information paradox: When AI platforms retain too much or too little data
Abstract: When do AI platforms retain too much or too little user data? Users disclose proprietary context to obtain useful generative-AI output, but retention of that context creates exposure and may improve future systems. We formalize this user-side analogue of Arrow’s information paradox. The disclosure cap separates two regimes. Outside the capped region, behavioral adjustment is strong enough for equilibrium harm to fall with retention, so the planner’s optimum is a boundary choice. Within the capped region, the ratio of benefit appropriability to harm internalization governs platform retention: the platform under-retains when the ratio is below one and over-retains when it is above one. When retained inputs also raise AI quality, retention and disclosure become complements once quality feedback is sufficiently strong. Retention regulation corrects the platform’s choice; an interior disclosure choice generally requires an additional disclosure-side instrument to implement the joint first best.

Title: How to determine key players when spillovers are large
Abstract: This paper examines the behavior of Katz–Bonacich centrality and key-player intercentrality in linear–quadratic network games when spillovers are large. This question is both important and empirically relevant, as it greatly simplifies the empirical testing of peer-effect models. We show that Katz–Bonacich centrality converges (up to scale) to the Perron eigenvector, while intercentrality diverges and loses all discriminatory power across nodes. Consequently, designing key-player policies becomes problematic: key-player rankings collapse, and no agent is more important than another when spillovers are sufficiently large.

Title: GVC participation and inflation in the European Union
Authors: Mariam Camarero, Antonia López-Villavicencio, Cecilio Tamarit
Abstract: This paper examines how participation in global value chains (GVCs) shapes inflation in the European Union over 1995–2023. Using local projections, we trace the dynamic response of producer- and consumer-price inflation to total, backward, and forward GVC shocks across core, peripheral, and CEEC economies. The aggregate response at the producer-price level is disinflationary and concentrated in the backward channel, supporting the discipline-on-prices hypothesis. A marked PPI–HICP wedge emerges in peripheral economies, where producer-level gains do not reach consumers, while forward linkages feed demand-pull pressures on consumer prices in both core and CEEC suppliers.

Title: Causal forests versus penalized splines for heterogeneous treatment effects
Authors: Ivan Korolev, Abiodun Musbaudeen, Nency Dhameja
Abstract: This paper compares causal forests with varying-coefficient penalized spline estimators for heterogeneous treatment effects. We conduct simulations with randomized treatment assignment that vary heterogeneity, predictor dimension, and discrete nuisance structure. Performance is measured by out-of-sample mean squared error. Forests perform best in Wager–Athey designs with sharp treatment-effect transitions. Penalized splines tend to dominate when heterogeneity is smooth, when the baseline mean and treatment effect differ in structure, and in mixed designs with continuous, binary, and group-level covariates. As group cardinality rises, forest performance deteriorates, while mgcv random-effect smooths handle group structure effectively and remain easy to implement.

Title: Tariff shocks and land sales: evidence from China’s cities
Abstract: This paper studies whether local governments use land sales to buffer trade shocks. Combining land transactions for 275 Chinese cities over 2015–2023 with a Bartik measure of US tariff exposure, we find that more exposed cities raise land-sale revenue after the US-China trade war through higher average prices rather than greater aggregate land area. The price increase reflects two channels: a shift toward high-grade land driven primarily by area expansion, and a within-use price increase in commercial-residential land with no corresponding area response. Mechanism analysis shows that tariff shocks weaken local economic activity and intensify fiscal pressure.

Title: Platform-wide agreements and competition for new users
Authors: Peter Boberg, Martino De Stefano, Keler Marku, Mary Beth Savio
Abstract: We study a bargaining model where a distributor allocates new users between an incumbent supplier, which also serves an installed base, and a rival. We compare separable agreements, whereby installed-base payments continue regardless of the new-user award, with platform-wide agreements, whereby those payments are made only if the incumbent receives the award. When installed-base users are inframarginal and bargaining is frictionless, the contractual linkage does not affect supplier selection or the rival’s equilibrium payment: the distributor’s lost payment is exactly offset by the incumbent’s avoided payment. When contracting frictions are present, platform-wide agreements can exclude a more efficient rival.

Title: Idle monetary policy? Evidence from monetary policy shocks for Pakistan
Authors: M. Ali Choudhary, Vasco J. Gabriel
Abstract: We challenge the narrative of idle monetary transmission in Pakistan. By cleansing conventional policy measures of anticipatory and endogenous motives à la Romer and Romer (2004), and using local projections in long differences (Jordá and Taylor, 2025; Piger and Stockwell, 2025), Piger and Stockwell, 2025], we trace the effects of monetary shocks on macroeconomic and financial outcomes while controlling for the global financial cycle (Miranda-Agrippino and Rey, 2020). A contractionary shock generates a large and persistent output contraction and a significant, non-monotone response of year-on-year inflation, with disinflation on impact and again after eight to nine quarters. The policy rate rises in the short run, while term-spread and credit responses are economically coherent but less precisely estimated. US monetary spillovers are small and statistically imprecise. Monetary policy works in Pakistan; only its measurement was idle.

Title: On the bracketing relationship in staggered treatment designs
Abstract: Researchers often use fixed-effects and lagged-dependent-variable (LDV) estimates as upper and lower bounds on a treatment effect. This paper studies this comparison in staggered-treatment designs and shows that the conventional ordering of the two estimates is not generally preserved. The direction of the difference depends on cohort- and event-time-specific treatment effects, outcome persistence, and the alignment of treatment timing with unit and time heterogeneity. Thus, either estimator may serve as the lower or upper bound, and the ordering may vary across group-time cells. Monte Carlo simulations further show that the interval formed by the two realized point estimates frequently fails to contain the true group-time average treatment effect in finite samples. The results suggest that fixed-effects and LDV estimates should be viewed as a descriptive comparison rather than as guaranteed bounds.

Title: Cryptocurrency uncertainty and bank intermediation
Abstract: The rapid expansion of cryptocurrency markets has intensified interactions between digital assets and traditional financial institutions, raising important questions about the implications of cryptocurrency-related uncertainty for banking activities. This paper investigates how cryptocurrency uncertainty shapes banks' funding, lending, and risk-taking decisions. Using a panel of 8330 banks across 129 countries over the period 2009–2018, we examine the relationship between cryptocurrency uncertainty and key dimensions of banks' balance-sheet decisions. We find that heightened cryptocurrency uncertainty increases customer deposits while reducing lending activity, non-performing loans, and risk-weighted assets. These findings suggest that banks respond to cryptocurrency uncertainty by adopting more conservative balance-sheet decisions characterized by stronger funding positions, lower credit expansion, and reduced risk exposure. The results remain robust to alternative measures of cryptocurrency uncertainty and lending activity. Our findings highlight that cryptocurrency uncertainty generates significant spillover effects on traditional financial intermediation and should be incorporated into macroprudential surveillance frameworks.

Title: What ties us together? Explaining synchronized GDP volatility
Authors: Javier Adrián López Artero, Lorenzo Ductor, Danilo Leiva-León
Abstract: Amidst heightened policy uncertainty, understanding the drivers of global macroeconomic instability becomes increasingly critical. This paper studies the determinants of output volatility synchronization using data for 42 economies worldwide. We construct a bilateral time-varying index of volatility synchronization and infer its drivers using Bayesian Model Averaging, complemented by Weighted Average Least Squares and LASSO. We find that differences in Total Factor Productivity, interest rate, and fiscal policy volatility robustly explain cross-country synchronization, with nuances between developed and developing countries. Overall, the results highlight the role of technological divergence and macroeconomic policy uncertainty in shaping the international co-movement of output volatility.

Title: Do stock markets price words or actions? President Donald Trump´s geopolitical signals and conflict risk
Abstract: Geopolitical tensions and military threats increasingly shape global financial markets. Using geopolitical threat signals associated with President Donald Trump, we distinguish between threats that later escalated into military action and those that did not. We find a clear asymmetry in stock market responses. Threats that do not materialize are associated with positive abnormal returns, whereas threats followed by military escalation generate weaker or negative effects, particularly in Latin American stock markets, while responses in G7 economies remain muted. These findings suggest that markets price not only geopolitical threats themselves, but also their perceived credibility and eventual realization, highlighting the role of credibility in asset pricing.

Title: Common ownership with a location leader
Authors: Kenneth Fjell, John S. Heywood, Debashis Pal
Abstract: We investigate the impact of common ownership in a spatial price discrimination model with sequential location choice. In contrast to simultaneous location choice, an increase in common ownership need not reduce locational efficiency. Common ownership by the location leader improves locational efficiency, even restoring the first best.

Title: Different institutions, different finance: Evidence from early twentieth-century China
Abstract: Institutional legacies are associated not only with the scale of finance but also with the organizational forms that emerge. Using prefecture-level data from early twentieth-century China, where indigenous money houses based on relational contracting coexisted with modern banks operating under codified law, we document that prefectures more deeply embedded in the imperial administrative system had more money houses and lower private borrowing costs, consistent with lower information and enforcement costs in relational finance. Treaty-port prefectures instead had more modern banks, with this concentration widening from 1910 to 1935. The analysis is descriptive and does not establish causality.

Title: Multiple testing in rolling-window analysis via p-value combination
Authors: Xing Ling, Qian Wu, Kun Chen
Abstract: Rolling-window methods are widely used to explore time variation in economic relationships. Testing across overlapping windows induces a multiple-testing problem and can inflate the familywise error. Existing corrections are often either overly conservative or computationally intensive. We propose a harmonic mean p[jls-end-space/]-value procedure that provides a global test together with window-level diagnostics. We establish iterated rejection-tail calibration of the global test and weak familywise error control for the associated diagnostic rule under overlap-induced dependence. Simulations using several standard time-series tests show accurate size, higher power, and substantially lower computational cost than bootstrap-based extreme-statistic procedures.

Title: Tourist taxation, Lerner symmetry, and the double dividend
Abstract: This paper studies a tax on tourism services, collected from foreign visitors upon entry, in a two-sector small open economy with congestible public infrastructure. Lerner symmetry implies that the tax raises manufacturing’s relative price and reverses tourism-driven Dutch disease. Tourism tax revenue lowers resident income taxes, while the contraction in tourism output reduces congestion, generating a double dividend.

Title: Birth rates, longevity, and monetary transmission
Abstract: The source of aging matters for the real-rate redistribution channel of monetary transmission in a three-generation life-cycle model. A given old-age dependency ratio can reflect higher longevity or a lower birth rate. We show that this channel depends on the source of aging and on who bears the fiscal cost, not on the ratio alone. When retirees bear a sufficiently large share of the fiscal cost, the low-birth-rate economy has the larger consumption response to a real interest-rate increase. Otherwise, the high-longevity economy has the larger response.

Title: Macroeconomic attention and stock market volatility: Evidence from dynamic forecast combinations
Abstract: We construct macroeconomic attention indicators (MAIs) using daily search engine data. Across multiple dynamic forecast combination approaches, the MAIs demonstrate significant predictive power for the realized volatility of the Chinese stock market. The predictive gains are primarily driven by attention to safe-haven demand (gold) and monetary policy (interest rates), with substantial heterogeneity across sectors. Moreover, MAIs become particularly informative during the high-uncertainty periods, highlighting the state-dependent transmission of macroeconomic attention to financial markets.

Title: Calibrating bid screens under quantity repricing
Abstract: Holding score fixed, unit-price bidders can reallocate line-item prices to hedge quantity risk. Repricing governs how this hedge affects realized payment, while a bid screen limits its size. Their interaction leaves residual exposure: baseline exposure minus effective hedge capacity, truncated at zero. Under constant absolute risk aversion (CARA), residual exposure generates a certainty-equivalent premium in the first-price score equilibrium. With a fixed binding screen, stronger repricing raises expected procurement payments when lost hedge capacity exceeds direct exposure relief. Calibrating the screen to preserve residual exposure preserves allocation, bidder utility, and expected payment under mean-level normalization.

Title: Symmetrized smooth test for the equality of distributions
Abstract: We develop a novel symmetrized smooth test for the equality of two distributions by incorporating information from two probability integral transform representations in a symmetric manner. This construction eliminates the dependence on the assignment of roles to the two samples. We establish the asymptotic Chi-square null distribution of the proposed symmetrized statistic and characterize its behavior under fixed and local alternatives. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed test achieves more stable size control and improved finite-sample performance, particularly when the sample sizes are small or unbalanced.

Title: Bounded rationality, monetary policy, and the scars of supply shocks
Authors: Dario Bonciani, Frantisek Masek, Paolo Nanni, Giulio Tarquini
Abstract: Bounded rationality reshapes monetary-policy trade-offs in response to supply shocks in a New Keynesian model with endogenous growth. A negative supply shock depresses innovation and future productivity, which gives rise to long-run scarring and persistent inflationary pressures. Under rational expectations, tighter monetary policy eases the initial rise in inflation but amplifies the fall in demand, innovation, and productivity. Under bounded rationality, households underreact to future income losses. This weakens the negative wealth effect and mitigates the decline in demand and growth. As a result, tighter monetary policy can contain inflation without generating large scarring effects.

Title: Do Ryder Cup captains randomize? Evidence from Sunday singles orders
Abstract: Professional sports offer rare field tests of game theory with observed choices, sharp incentives, and expert competitors. Ryder Cup Sunday singles is a simultaneous permutation game where captains order twelve players and pairings form slot by slot. Under Hurley (2002)’s benchmark, uniform random ordering is a mixed-strategy equilibrium of the constant-sum game, and therefore also a minimax strategy. Using Sunday singles orders from 1981–2025 and, where available, Data Golf and OWGR ranks before each Cup, I test whether within-team ability is assigned uniformly at random across lineup slots. Permutation tests reject uniform random assignment. The data indicate that stronger players appear earlier than random shuffles within teams predict, with the pattern more pronounced in later Ryder Cups.

Title: Bank market power and fire-sale amplification under earnings-based constraints
Abstract: This paper analyzes the macroeconomic consequences of bank market power under corporate earnings-based borrowing constraints. By embedding a Cournot banking structure within a Kiyotaki-Moore framework, we uncover a sharp structural reversal: while credit market power dampens the fire-sale multiplier under traditional asset-backed constraints, it amplifies that multiplier under earnings covenants. The endogenous lending markup directly inflates debt-service obligations, tightening borrowers’ cash-flow constraints, forcing deeper asset misallocations and severe aggregate output contractions. Fostering banking competition and relaxing countercyclical covenants act as structural complements, compressing spreads and maximizing real capital retention during financial distress.

Title: On competitive equilibria and cores in housing market problem with one broker
Abstract: In the classical housing market problem, when all agents have strict preferences, Roth and Postlewaite (1977) show that the top trading cycles (TTC) mechanism yields the unique competitive equilibrium allocation and the unique strong core allocation. We study an extension of the housing market model that incorporates one broker. We propose the concepts of competitive equilibrium and strong core, and show that the outcome yielded by the trading cycles mechanism in Pycia and Ünver (2017) is the unique competitive equilibrium allocation and the unique strong core allocation.

Title: A note on the asymptotic unbiasedness of Akaike information criterion
Authors: Yong Li, Zhou Wu, Jun Yu, Tao Zeng
Abstract: This note revisits the standard derivation of the asymptotic unbiasedness of Akaike information criterion (AIC). The existing literature has shown that AIC is an asymptotically unbiased estimator of the predictive risk. However, there is a technical issue in these justifications. In this note, we bridge the gap and establish the asymptotic unbiasedness of AIC under certain regularity conditions, which are applicable in various scenarios. Our result suggests that AIC should be used with caution if the moment conditions on the parameter estimators may not hold. When model misspecification is allowed, our result can be extended to Takeuchi information criterion (TIC).

Title: When patents become collateral: Intellectual property financialization and corporate venture capital investment
Abstract: This paper examines whether patent-backed financing reforms affect firms’ external technology acquisition strategies. Using the staggered rollout of China’s Patent Pledge Financing Pilot (PPFP) across cities, we employ a difference-in-differences design to study its effect on corporate venture capital (CVC) investment. We find that PPFP significantly increases firms’ CVC activity, with the effect concentrated in high-tech CVC, and weaker for state-owned enterprises. These findings are consistent with the view that increasing the financial value of patent assets strengthens firms’ incentives to engage in technology-oriented CVC for external technology sourcing.

Title: The Phillips multiplier and the two sides of inflation
Abstract: The inflation-unemployment trade-off faced by a central bank can be characterised non-parametrically by the Phillips multiplier of Barnichon and Mesters (2021). Because the multiplier is linear in inflation, it inherits any exact decomposition of it. We split it into the two directional margins of price adjustment of Quineche and Zapata (2026). Before 1990, a policy-induced one-percentage-point rise in the cumulative unemployment gap raises cumulative deflationary pressure by 0.4pp: the identified trade-off runs through price cuts. After 1990, excluding the zero lower bound, nothing is identified: neither the multiplier nor either margin. The instruments carry too little exogenous variation.

Title: Protecting employees or replacing them? Paid sick leave mandates and firm automation
Abstract: Paid sick leave mandates aim to improve employee benefits. This paper examines how firms respond to the additional labor costs caused by PSL mandates. Leveraging the staggered implementation of PSL mandates across U.S. states, we use a difference-in-differences design and find that mandatory PSLs greatly accelerate firms’ adoption of automation. This effect is particularly evident among labor-intensive firms, consistent with the view that rising employment costs drive labor-capital substitution. Overall, by revealing an unintended consequence of PSL mandates, this study contributes to the pertinent literature and has important policy implications.

Title: Supplier competition and the incentive to purchase data
Authors: Huaxin Huang, Na Leng, Jian Ni
Abstract: We investigate suppliers’ incentive to purchase data in a supply chain where multiple competing suppliers face uncertain downstream demand and may choose to acquire noisy demand signals (data) to improve their decisions. We identify a competition-reinforcement effect: data acquisition can trigger more aggressive competition among suppliers, which in turn erodes their incentive to purchase data. We show that this competition reinforcement effect could outweigh the conventional informed-decision benefit of better demand information, especially when input substitutability is low. As a result, intensified competition could reduce suppliers’ willingness to buy data, and may even generate net welfare losses.

Title: Strategy uniqueness and stock price crash risk
Abstract: This paper examines how corporate strategy uniqueness influences stock price crash risk. Using portfolio analyses and panel regressions, we find that firms pursuing more unique strategies exhibit significantly lower crash risk. Channel analyses suggest that strategically unique firms face lower competitive pressure and weaker incentives to withhold bad news, thereby mitigating crash risk. Cross-sectional results further indicate that this negative relationship is stronger among firms with greater information asymmetry and weaker corporate governance. Overall, our findings provide important evidence on the role of corporate strategy in shaping firms’ downside tail risk.

Title: Do non-binding trade promotion partnerships create trade? Evidence from UK–US state memoranda of understanding
Abstract: Governments increasingly use soft, non-binding trade promotion partnerships alongside, or instead of, binding agreements, but their effects remain unclear. This paper studies the UK’s post-Brexit memoranda of understanding with individual US states. These partnerships promote trade and investment but cannot alter tariffs or establish enforceable market-access commitments. Using a structural gravity model and monthly state level goods trade data, we find no evidence of broad goods trade creation. Aggregate effects are insignificant, and product- and state-level estimates are heterogeneous rather than systematically positive, suggesting MoUs support economic cooperation rather than producing the broad trade effects associated with traditional binding agreements.

Title: An auditable AI agent loop for empirical economics: A case study in forecast combination
Abstract: AI coding agents, general purpose assistants that write and execute code, make empirical specification search fast and cheap, but they also widen hidden researcher degrees of freedom. This paper adapts an open-source agent-loop architecture to an empirical economics workflow and adds a post-search holdout evaluation. In a forecast-combination illustration, independent agent searches find methods that improve on benchmarks from the original study. Logged search and holdout evaluation together make adaptive specification search more transparent and help distinguish robust improvements from sample-specific discoveries.

Title: AI innovation and labor market polarization: Evidence from European regions
Authors: Antonio Minniti, Klaus Prettner, Francesco Venturini
Abstract: We study whether AI innovation changes labor-market polarization by weakening the relative position of high-skilled workers. We develop a CES production framework showing how AI affects the wage-cost ratio between high- and low-skilled workers through wage and employment margins. We test the model’s predictions using European regional labor-market data and find that AI reduces the relative wage-cost ratio by nearly 7 percent on average, with effects broadly split between wage and employment adjustments. These results are primarily driven by regions in countries highly specialized in AI technologies. Overall, our evidence suggests that AI may counteract the polarization effects associated with over two centuries of technological change.

Title: Competitive shield or carbon burden? Evidence from equity market reactions to CBAM enforcement
Abstract: This paper examines equity market reactions to the enforcement of the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) on January 1, 2026. Using an event-study approach on a sample of S&P 500 and STOXX Europe 600 firms, we document three main findings. First, CBAM enforcement is associated with positive aggregate abnormal returns, consistent with the resolution of policy uncertainty. Second, both European firms and CBAM-exposed sectors experience lower post-event returns on average, reflecting compliance costs. Third, and most importantly, the interaction between geography and CBAM exposure shows that the impact of exposure is relatively more favorable for European firms compared to their U.S. counterparts. These results suggest that CBAM is perceived by financial markets as both a carbon burden and a competitive mechanism, with effects concentrated in the short run.

Title: Policy incentives, firm investment, and debt rollover risk
Abstract: We develop a real options model with finite-maturity debt to examine how rollover risk shapes the relative effectiveness of tax cuts and investment subsidies. Shorter debt maturity amplifies rollover risk, which strengthens the effectiveness of tax cuts while weakening that of investment subsidies. Under budget neutrality, tax cuts are always optimal. Under a net-subsidy regime, the optimal instrument is maturity-dependent: subsidies are optimal at long maturities, while as maturity shortens, a threshold tax rate emerges above which tax cuts are optimal and below which subsidies remain optimal. When maturity is sufficiently short, tax cuts dominate across all tax rates.

Title: Free to move? Immigration liberalization and international migration
Abstract: This paper examines how immigration liberalization affects migrant inflows. We exploit Switzerland’s gradual introduction of free movement for European Union and European Free Trade Association nationals, while third-country nationals remained subject to a selective quota-based regime. Using administrative register data and a staggered difference-in-differences design, we find that free movement substantially increased immigration from affected countries, with the preferred specification implying that immigration more than doubled on average.

Title: Trade agreements, trade facilitation and mutual recognition arrangements
Abstract: Governments use preferential trade agreements (PTAs), the WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement (TFA) and mutual recognition arrangements (MRAs) to reduce bilateral trade costs. Using data for 2010-2022 and a structural gravity framework, we assess the trade impact of a country-pair using all three policy instruments simultaneously. Our analysis considers MRAs for Authorized Economic Operator (AEO) programs that expedite customs clearance for certified actors in the supply chain. These are not product-specific, permitting comparative analysis of the trade impacts of the three types of international agreements. We find significant sectoral heterogeneity across the three instruments. The TFA has large effects on bilateral trade in non-food manufacturing products, while MRAs do more to boost the value of trade in agricultural and food-related products. Overall, international cooperation to reduce the costs of regulatory heterogeneity increases bilateral trade more than PTAs.

Title: Geopolitics and space access: cost asymmetries and strategic dependence
Abstract: Access to space is now a national security priority, yet its cost varies enormously across nations. Using a novel dataset of over 6,740 rocket launches (1960–2025), we estimate country-level launch costs and country-specific experience curves. In 2025, the average costs per kilogram to Low Earth Orbit ranged from $3,225 in the United States to over $13,000 in India, with Europe, Russia, China, and Japan in between. Since 2010, only the US and Europe display statistically significant experience curves, with the US improving far faster. These widening asymmetries reinforce strategic dependencies with economic and security implications.

Title: Dictator game giving: Money vs. effort — women are more generous with money but more selfish with effort
Authors: Petr Krautwurm, Lena von Deylen, Philipp C. Wichardt
Abstract: The data reported in this paper show that dictator game transfers depend crucially on whether money or effort are to be distributed. In a standard (monetary) version, giving is far more generous (close to equal sharing); behaviour is highly selfish in the effort version. Moreover, women are more altruistic then men when distributing money but are more selfish when distributing effort. The results suggest that the common focus on monetary transfers covers only part of the story.

Title: Monetary policy transmission under supply-chain disruptions: Evidence from a time-varying BVAR
Abstract: This paper examines the time-varying effects of monetary policy and global supply-chain disruptions on U.S. inflation and GDP during the COVID-19 pandemic. To this end, we estimate a time-varying parameter Bayesian Vector Autoregressive (TVP-BVAR) model. We find that expansionary monetary policy shocks’ impact differs significantly between pre- and post-pandemic periods. Specifically, inflationary effects of supply-chain disruptions increased substantially after the pandemic, while output effects remained stable. Furthermore, monetary policy pass-through to inflation strengthens as supply-chain pressures intensify. Finally, statistical evidence shows that supply-chain disruptions steepen the Phillips curve, with the effect most pronounced for durable goods inflation.

Title: Do prediction markets price events or adjudication? Evidence from the disputed Polymarket markets
Abstract: A prediction-market share is read as a probability about an event. In an oracle-settled market the cash flow is fixed not by the event but by the outcome that the resolution mechanism certifies, so the price can come apart from the event. We test whether prices forecast the event or the adjudication by reading them inside the on-chain settlement window of disputed Polymarket markets, the interval between a bonded proposer’s assertion of the outcome and the UMA token vote that fixes the payoff. Inside that window the real-world event is already frozen while the payoff is still pending, so a discount on the asserted-correct claim cannot be ordinary forecasting of an unrealized event. Using 233 disputed markets with a clear audited rule-correct winner, coded by a search-grounded language-model audit formed independently of how the oracle ruled and matched to each market’s UMA Optimistic Oracle lifecycle, we find the token vote overturns the audited winner in 12.4 percent of markets, an upper bound inherited from the coding model. Six hours after the first dispute the audited-correct claim already trades at a discount that is 0.83 higher in markets the oracle will overturn, and the discount climbs toward one as the vote approaches while the upheld claim falls toward zero. The pricing pattern survives the choice of coding model, the removal of deadline questions, restriction to the markets that escalate to the vote, and a treatment limited to the hand-verified overturns. The complete UMA voting record shows the deciding votes to be broad and near unanimous, and the dispute-time price predicts the vote share itself. Prices in contested prediction markets are therefore best read not as beliefs about the world but as forecasts of how a decentralized rule will be adjudicated.

Title: Point scale framing and student performance: Evidence from a field experiment
Authors: Puneet Arora, Arihant Jain, Ishita Tripathi
Abstract: Does the numerical scale used to score an exam affect how hard students try? We test this question with a preregistered natural field experiment in which 1235 university students in India took identical tests framed as scored out of either 20 or 100 points. Exploiting both a high-stakes graded quiz and a zero-stakes additional test, we find no statistically or economically meaningful effects of the point-scale manipulation on test scores or on four effort measures, regardless of stakes, gender, or prior ability. These consistently null results, robust across settings, outcomes, and subgroups, identify a boundary condition for the numerosity heuristic: when scoring units are transparently arbitrary and evaluation ultimately rests on percentages, numerical rescaling does not shift behavior. The findings support the behavioral neutrality of a widely used and easily modified feature of assessment design.

Title: Gender differences in teacher grading across school subjects: Evidence from Germany
Abstract: This study examines whether gender differences in teacher-assigned grades vary systematically across subjects. Using data from German secondary schools, I compare teacher-assigned grades with anonymously graded standardized test scores within a difference-in-differences framework. Across six core subjects spanning the humanities and STEM, I find systematic grading differentials favoring female students. The estimated differential is largest in German and Math and substantially smaller in English and the sciences, indicating considerable cross-subject heterogeneity. The differential also varies markedly by school track and teacher experience, with systematically larger estimates in the academic track and particularly pronounced differentials among novice teachers.

Title: Revisiting patience and achievement: evidence from matched parent–child preferences
Abstract: This paper examines whether children’s time preferences independently predict academic achievement using matched incentivized measures for parents and children linked to standardized mathematics performance. Reduced-form regressions replicate prior findings that more patient children perform better academically. However, once parental time preferences are included, children’s patience no longer predicts achievement, while parental patience remains strongly significant across specifications. These results suggest that previously documented links between children’s time preferences and academic performance may reflect intergenerational behavioral transmission or household inputs rather than child-specific traits. The findings highlight the importance of jointly modeling parent and child characteristics when studying non-cognitive skill formation.

Title: A single-axiom cardinal characterisation of quadratic utility
Abstract: In the cardinal part of their analysis of spherical preferences, Chambers and Echenique (2020) characterise quadratic-plus-linear utility using two axioms concerning changes from a status quo: Status Quo Independence (SQI) and Eventual Linearity (EL). We show that the two axioms are not independent. Specifically, SQI implies EL and, indeed, forces the additivity condition in EL to hold at every status quo, not merely at some status quo. Consequently, under continuity and normalisation, SQI alone characterises the representation, implying that their cardinal theorem remains valid when EL is dropped. The respective roles of continuity and normalisation are also clarified.

Title: Limited awareness and message feasibility in cheap talk
Authors: Zhonghao Shui, Beiqing Cui, Jian Wu
Abstract: This note studies how limited awareness affects cheap talk through message feasibility. A receiver is already aware of a new state, while the sender may be unable to formulate the associated message. We characterize monotone informative equilibria in a three-state game where the sender becomes aware of the new state with an exogenous probability before observing the payoff-relevant state. Prior awareness partially restores the common-awareness mimicking constraint. The new-state message may identify the payoff-relevant state, combine state and awareness information, or remain informative by revealing the sender's awareness even when it no longer identifies the state.

Title: Application fees and the robustness of Nash equilibria in school choice
Abstract: We study the robustness of Nash equilibria in the preference revelation game induced by the student-optimal stable mechanism when small application fees are introduced. Assuming lexicographic preferences over outcomes, we show that introducing application fees reduces the set of Nash equilibria, to the detriment of student welfare. We provide a sufficient condition on the distribution of application fees that eliminates any Pareto improvement in which a student strictly benefits from being assigned to a given school. When all application fees are strictly positive for all applications, every Nash equilibrium induces a stable assignment.

Title: Warm-glow bequests and descendant risk
Abstract: Reduced-form bequest motives are routinely assumed to exhibit decreasing absolute risk aversion (DARA). I show this is consistent with an underlying altruistic primitive: when descendant risk is unrealised at the bequest choice date, DARA of the warm-glow preference is inherited from the descendant’s continuation value under both multiplicative and additive risk, without parametric restriction. Yet the two canonical specifications differ in what is preserved beyond DARA. Multiplicative risk yields a shifter-weight decomposition and preserves CRRA form; additive income risk—the relevant case for dynastic precautionary savings—preserves DARA but not functional form.

Title: Narrow non-bank financial intermediation and economic growth: does the economic cycle matter?
Abstract: In this paper, we examine whether the relationship between non-bank financial intermediation (NBFI) and economic growth varies across the economic cycle. While existing studies focus on the average effects of broad measures of NBFI, the effects of the narrow measure of NBFI differing during periods of economic stress is less clear. Using a panel of 26 jurisdictions participating in the Financial Stability Board's NBFI exercise between 2006 and 2024, we find that larger narrow NBFI sectors are associated with higher real GDP growth. However, we find limited evidence that this relationship varies systematically between expansionary and recessionary periods.

Title: Learning from observed matches in two-sided markets
Abstract: This paper asks what can be learned from observed merger pairings when acquirers and targets meet in a two-sided market with transferable utility. A compact assignment-game model implies revealed-preference inequalities: observed matches must generate at least as much total surplus as feasible counterfactual matches in the same local market. I take these inequalities to Refinitiv M&A data for U.S. same-industry transactions during 2010–2024. The final estimation sample contains 1025 completed acquirer-target pairs and 36,881 financially feasible counterfactual pairs constructed within industry-quarter cells. A benchmark linear surplus specification based on differences in profitability, leverage, sales growth, and liquidity has weak identifying content. Across 60 optimization runs, the same maximum score is obtained, but the coefficient vectors attaining it differ substantially in sign and magnitude. The result is not a general impossibility claim about revealed-preference methods. It shows that observed matches and standard financial differences alone provide limited discipline on merger surplus when transfers, outside options, and richer pair-specific synergies are unobserved.

Title: Endogenous networks with constrained public goods
Abstract: This paper incorporates individual effort constraints into a network formation framework with local public goods. Strict Nash equilibria are characterised, featuring complete multipartite networks as a novel class of stratified structures, where agents are organised into distinct layers based on heterogeneous effort levels, with full inter-layer connectivity and no intra-layer links. We further show that such constraints weaken the law of the few by limiting extreme concentration of effort provision. As a result, equilibrium networks exhibit broader participation in production and layered patterns of effort provision.

Title: Interest rates and bank runs
Abstract: We study how high short-term interest rates affect depositor withdrawals and bank fragility. In a global games model, depositors choose between bank deposits and money market funds, while bank holds short-term and long-term assets. Higher rates raise the payoff from withdrawing and reduce long-term asset recovery values. The model delivers a critical interest rate threshold above which runs occur, conditional on bank balance-sheet fundamentals. Lower switching cost, weaker long-term asset returns, larger fire-sale loss, and larger long-term asset share lower the threshold and expand the run region.

Title: Target-driven Bayesian stacking of realised and implied volatility forecasts
Authors: Hongfei Guo, J.M. Marín, Helena Veiga
Abstract: We propose target-driven Bayesian stacking for a fixed six-model ensemble of GARCH and stochastic-volatility forecasts with realised- and VIX-based extensions. Two rolling stacking rules target either log predictive density or QLIKE. In S&P 500, the objective changes the preferred information channel: LPD stacking remains centred on GARCH-RV, whereas QLIKE stacking shifts toward GARCH-VIX. Across 56 rolling windows, the QLIKE stack improves certainty-equivalent returns by roughly one to one-and-a-half percentage points per year, depending on the investor’s risk aversion. In the 30 windows where the QLIKE stack assigns material weight to implied volatility models, the gain exceeds two percentage points per year with a 90% win rate. However, LPD stacking delivers tighter 5% Value-at-Risk calibration.

Title: Why efficient systems fail spectacularly: A unified theory of systemic risk
Abstract: I develop a unified model of resource and risk sharing in which N agents pool against a common crisis threshold subject to transaction costs. Three results follow. As transaction costs fall: the welfare-optimal pool expands and individual buffers shrink; average welfare improves strictly; and expected crisis scale — the number of agents simultaneously unable to access the shared resource — grows, even if crisis probability falls. The mechanism is identical across financial risk pooling, supply-chain management, and transportation networks. Large systemic crises are the necessary consequence of welfare-optimal pooling. The correct policy response is a Pigouvian charge on each participant’s marginal contribution to expected crisis scale.

Title: Effects of oil price uncertainty on the stock returns of oil and gas companies
Authors: Elena Maria Diaz, Juncal Cunado, Fernando Perez de Gracia
Abstract: This paper investigates the distinct effects of oil-specific and global uncertainty shocks on the stock returns of international oil and gas companies. Using monthly data from May 2007 to August 2025, we employ a Dynamic Factor Model on high-frequency volatility indices to construct separate proxies for global uncertainty and idiosyncratic oil uncertainty shocks. The dynamic effects of these shocks are estimated using Smoothed Local Projections. Global uncertainty shocks generate an immediate and homogeneous decline in stock returns across integrated, upstream, and downstream firms. In contrast, the effects of oil-specific uncertainty depend on a firm’s position within the value chain. Upstream firms exhibit the most pronounced responses, integrated firms display intermediate and mixed effects, while downstream companies appear comparatively insulated from oil-market uncertainty. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing global from sector-specific uncertainty when assessing the financial consequences of uncertainty shocks in energy markets.

Title: Geopolitical risk and inflation: Does central bank independence matter?
Authors: Whelsy Boungou, Stevy Darel Moussavou Moussavou, Bossoma Doriane N’Doua
Abstract: Does central bank independence shape the inflationary impact of geopolitical risk? Using a panel of 29 countries over 1990–2023, we show that geopolitical risk significantly increases inflation, but that this effect depends on the degree of central bank independence. Higher institutional credibility substantially attenuates, and in some case offsets, the inflationary impact of geopolitical shocks. This moderating effect is stronger for geopolitical threats than for realized actions and is considerably more pronounced in advanced than in emerging economies. These findings highlight the importance of credible monetary institutions in enhancing resilience to geopolitical inflation.

Title: Diagnostic testing a time series regression with zero-one dummies
Abstract: We consider tests for normality, residual autocorrelation, and autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity for a time series regression, which includes various zero-one dummy variables for individual observations. The sizes of these tests are distorted as the residuals associated with the dummies are equal to zero. We propose a simple solution which amounts to dismissing the observations with these zero-valued residuals, that is, treat these observations as missing. With simulations we show that the resulting tests have the proper size.

Title: Improved Andrews’ formula for testing changing mean
Authors: Wei Li, Xinyue Zhang, Yang Zu
Abstract: We propose a robust bandwidth rule for the classical CUSUM and QS tests for shifts in the mean of a time series: the AR(1) coefficient entering Andrews’ (1991) data-driven HAC bandwidth is truncated at a fixed threshold (Formula presented), with ρ0 selected by a simulation-based procedure that controls empirical size against a user-specified persistence robustness target. The truncated bandwidth is shown to be free from the asymptotic power reversal problem under the diverging-alternatives framework of Juhl and Xiao (2009). Monte Carlo evidence indicates that the CUSUM and QS tests implemented with this bandwidth deliver good size control and monotonic power across a range of break designs and persistence levels.

Title: Efficiency bounds for incomplete information social interaction models with network structures
Abstract: This paper studies incomplete information social interaction models with exogenous network structures under rational expectations, where an agent’s outcome is affected by the expected outcomes of other agents through a network. Incomplete information models are suitable for cases where an agent’s outcome is not fully observed or precisely predictable to others. Under an asymptotic framework with many small networks, we derive efficiency bounds for the model. The derivation requires the information matrix to be non-singular. We show that the information matrix is non-singular under an identification condition based on observed network structures.

Title: Three horizon-specific drivers of gold prices with Iterated Dynamic Model Averaging
Authors: Sihan Chen, Shenggang Yang, Xiaomei Lan
Abstract: This paper identifies three monthly horizon-specific drivers of gold prices using Iterated Dynamic Model Averaging (IDMA), a new machine-learning method that optimizes DMA by cyclically selecting predictors and updating forgetting factors. IDMA and standard DMA outperform other benchmarks, validating the variable selection mechanism. Predictor selection reveals three main drivers: stock market spillovers over short term, interest rate factors over the medium to long term, and safe-haven effects against geopolitical risk over long term. With the financialization of commodities, spillover effects from equity markets have become more prominent in gold price dynamics, challenging gold’s traditional safe-haven role in financial markets.

Title: Do non-financial risks compound? Evidence from U.S. industry returns
Abstract: Non-financial risks affect asset prices individually, yet they are typically studied in isolation. Using 49 Fama–French industry portfolios over 1990–2026, we show that pairwise compound channels among geopolitical risk, climate policy uncertainty, and financial stress carry significant pricing power beyond individual exposures. Climate policy uncertainty emerges as the nexus variable: its interaction with financial conditions is the most consistent channel, surviving all standard error methods, sub-sample splits, and predetermined (lagged) financial conditions, with an effect roughly four times larger for carbon-intensive industries. A Wald test confirms the joint significance of the interactions while individual risks lack joint significance.

Title: Omitted instrument bias
Abstract: Researchers often have access to multiple instrumental variables for a single treatment, yet empirical practice frequently relies on only one instrument while ignoring the others. We show that this approach generally identifies a noncausal parameter. We characterize the resulting “omitted-instrument bias” and show that it vanishes in special cases, such as when instruments are independent of each other or treatment effects are homogeneous. We propose a simple alternative two-stage least squares specification that identifies a causal estimand.

Title: Maximum resale prices across heterogeneous local markets
Abstract: We study maximum resale prices across heterogeneous local markets that share a common target retail price. A sufficiently small retailer margin can make the ceiling bind across markets, allowing common terms to implement this price. Two-part tariffs instead require the marginal wholesale price to align the retailer’s unconstrained optimal price exactly with the target. If the ceiling already binds, changes in market structure require no contractual recalibration. Apple’s use of list prices as de facto maximum resale prices, combined with discounts from those prices for independent resellers, illustrates a setting in which the mechanism may be relevant.

Title: On the inefficiency and coalitional manipulability of stable mechanisms
Authors: Gabriela J. Denis, Juan Pablo Torres-Martínez
Abstract: In the context of school choice, Ergin (2002) shows that Pareto efficiency and group strategy-proofness are equivalent properties for the student-optimal stable mechanism. We show that this equivalence holds at each preference profile and for every stable mechanism, providing a simple test for coalitional manipulability.

Title: Corporate earnings announcements and stock market bubbles
Authors: Elie Bouri, Ufuk Can, Oguzhan Cepni, Rangan Gupta
Abstract: We examine how corporate earnings announcement shocks influence US stock market bubbles using daily data from January 1990 to June 2025. After identifying positive and negative bubbles, we derive corporate earnings announcement shocks using a heteroskedastic vector autoregression model and estimate their dynamic effects on bubble indicators using local projections, with vector autoregression-based impulse responses reported as a robustness check. Positive earnings shocks boost positive bubbles, particularly at the medium to long-term, while reducing negative bubbles at the short-term. Therefore, favorable earnings news can fuel prolonged speculative episodes by increasing investor optimism, and lead to deep crashes but mild recoveries.

Title: Low-cost AI and the value of compute scarcity: Evidence from the DeepSeek shock
Abstract: We study whether the DeepSeek-R1 shock changed the market value of scarce AI compute. Using U.S. stock returns around January 27, 2025 and compute-supply exposure from pre-event 10-K filings, firms more exposed to supplying AI compute earned significantly lower abnormal returns. In the preferred specification, higher compute-supply exposure predicts a 2.37 percentage-point lower three-day cumulative abnormal return (CAR[-1,+1]). Results survive industry fixed effects, risk and financial controls, alternative benchmarks, placebo dates, and text-validation checks. The evidence suggests DeepSeek was priced as a shock to AI compute scarcity rents, not only a broad technology-sector shock.

Title: The dismal theorem in a general equilibrium climate-economy model
Authors: Christoph Hambel, Frederick van der Ploeg
Abstract: We show that Weitzman (2009)’s dismal theorem resurfaces naturally within a dynamic asset pricing framework with temperature-related disaster risk. If the climate disaster loss distribution is sufficiently fat-tailed, the risk-adjusted expected loss term diverges. Under unit elasticity of intertemporal substitution (EIS), this causes the social cost of carbon (SCC) to explode and the underlying optimization problem to have no finite solution so that the dynamic general equilibrium analogue of the dismal theorem applies. We show that, if the risk of climate tipping increases with temperature, the fat tail becomes endogenous and the dismal result is more likely to be activated at higher temperatures.

Title: The two clocks of systemic importance
Abstract: Systemic importance has two dimensions, a bank’s contribution to system-wide tail risk (Δ[jls-end-space/]CoVaR) and its exposure to it (marginal expected shortfall, MES). Using daily Δ[jls-end-space/]CoVaR and MES for 24 publicly traded Global Systemically Important Banks over 2012–2025, we show the two rankings move on different clocks. Contribution rankings reorder at the same rate in calm times, the pandemic, and after. Exposure rankings survive the pandemic but re-anchor sharply at the 2022–2023 interest-rate regime change, as euro-area banks fall and US and Japanese banks rise. Shocks rotate which banks contribute to systemic risk; only regime changes move which are exposed.

Title: The growing importance of universities for patenting and innovation
Abstract: We document a growing link between university R&D expenditures and patenting activity in surrounding metropolitan statistical areas (MSAs) since 1980: the patents-per-capita gap between MSAs with and without a research university has doubled, and the elasticity of patents with respect to university R&D has tripled. We present several pieces of evidence showing that this trend reflects growing spillovers from universities: it is robust to MSA and university characteristics; local invention tracks the content of nearby university research; and the link is stronger where universities do more basic research. Thus, universities may increasingly shape the geography of innovation.

Title: Parameter-invariant unbiased estimation of individual variances and their pairwise products
Abstract: Recent literature proposed variants of estimators of conditional error variances that are robust to the presence of many regressors. One of the proposals produces unbiased estimates, which, however, are sensitive to regression parameter values. We propose its modification based on cross-fitting and averaging over random sample splits, which preserves the unbiasedness but eliminates that sensitivity. Then, we extend the cross-fitting machinery to unbiased estimation of pairwise variance products and to testing for many restrictions. We verify properties of associated estimators and tests in a simulation setup with many covariates.

Title: The reset premium: Option value under asymmetric price commitment
Abstract: We show that a one-sided price-adjustment rule, with free price cuts but a fixed daily reset for price increases, raises the reset price even under risk neutrality, mean-zero wholesale cost shocks, and perfect consumer information. The mechanism is option-theoretic: a higher reset price preserves pass-through in adverse cost states, while favorable shocks can still be accommodated by price cuts. In differentiated Bertrand competition, the reset premium scales with cost pass-through and hence with substitutability. The mechanism is distinct from consumer search and strategic price dispersion because it operates even under perfect consumer price information.

Title: Peer-confirming equilibrium in anchor games
Abstract: Peer-confirming equilibrium (Lipnowski and Sadler, 2019) weakens Nash equilibrium: given a network, each player correctly anticipates only her neighbors’ actions. We relate the two in anchor games, in which one player—the anchor—is indifferent among her actions, while every other player’s unique best response varies one-to-one with the anchor’s action. We show that peer-confirming equilibrium coincides with Nash equilibrium if and only if the network is connected. Even when a neighbor’s action is payoff-irrelevant, so long as it reveals the action of a payoff-relevant player, that information is transmitted exactly across any distance.

Title: Voting in the heat of the moment: Climate change salience and electoral behavior
Authors: Rafael Araujo, Leila Pereira, Rogerio Santarrosa
Abstract: We examine the impact of short-term temperature changes on voting behavior in the Brazilian presidential elections from 2010 to 2018, focusing on the candidacy of Marina Silva, a prominent pro-environment politician. Using data on municipality level voting and daily wet bulb temperature, we find that an increase in temperature on election day increases votes for Marina Silva. We argue that this effect is driven by the salience of climate change issues, which influences last-minute voting decisions. Our analysis also shows that temperature variations in the days preceding the election have a limited impact on voting outcomes, highlighting the transient nature of climate salience effects.

Title: Generative AI-assisted investor communication and stock price crash risk
Abstract: This study examines the effect of managerial responses assisted by generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) on stock price crash risk. Using question–response data from investor-relations platforms operated by Chinese stock exchanges, we employ large language models (LLMs) to measure the degree of GenAI assistance in managerial responses. We find that stronger GenAI-assisted textual features predict higher future stock price crash risk. We further show that greater response–question mismatch and more negative investor sentiment serve as two potential mechanisms, and that the effect is more pronounced among firms with more frequent investor interactions.

Title: Systematic forecast errors from extreme weather events in credit risk models
Abstract: Extreme weather events generate systematic forecast errors in credit risk models. Using proprietary loan-level data covering approximately 250,000 corporate loans over 2012–2023, we find that exposure to extreme weather significantly predicts realized default rates after conditioning on model-implied probabilities. Effects are stronger for early-year exposures and reflect persistent regional vulnerability rather than transitory fluctuations. These results suggest that omitted climate risk factors contribute to systematic model miscalibration, robust across specifications. More broadly, when relevant weather events are excluded, forecast errors may become systematic rather than idiosyncratic, with implications for model design and the efficient allocation of credit.

Title: The capital-access premium and the won: Korean stablecoin premia as a leading indicator of exchange-rate pressure
Abstract: On Korean cryptocurrency exchanges, dollar-pegged stablecoins trade above their dollar value at the market exchange rate. In the primary USDT/KRW sample used in this paper, the average premium is 1.96%. Because stablecoins are designed to maintain a one-dollar value, their won premium offers a direct market measure of dollar-access pressure under segmented crypto-FX markets. Using 919 daily observations from 7 December 2023 to 12 June 2026, we show that the premium co-moves closely with the Bitcoin kimchi premium and predicts won depreciation over the next one to three days. The relation survives controls for realized USD/KRW volatility, VIX, dollar strength, and domestic equity-market conditions. Coefficients are larger in high-VIX and high-FX-volatility regimes, but the short sample calls for caution. Stablecoin premia may provide a timely gauge of exchange-rate pressure in segmented markets.

Title: Geopolitics and the strait of Hormuz: Evidence from Middle East stock markets
Authors: Mondher Bouattour, Amine Ben Amar, Emilios Galariotis, Néjib Hachicha
Abstract: This letter examines the impact of the 2026 Iran conflict and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz on Middle Eastern Stock Markets. The findings reveal heterogeneous effects across the region, with the largest market responses concentrated in Qatar, the UAE, and Egypt. Sectoral analysis further reveals varied gradual adjustment dynamics across industries, with the real estate, healthcare, consumer discretionary, consumer staples and financial sectors exhibiting the largest declines. These results highlight the rapid transmission of geopolitical risk across regional financial markets and underscore the vulnerability of Gulf economies to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

Title: The tragedy of the horizon: A contracting account
Abstract: The “tragedy of the horizon” captures the gap between long-horizon climate damages and the shorter horizons of corporate decision-making. We provide a contracting account of this idea using a deliberately standard CARA-normal moral-hazard model. Under full commitment, the optimal linear contract can condition on long-horizon outcomes; horizon mismatch alone does not generate underinvestment. The tragedy arises when shareholders cannot credibly commit today to compensate a CEO based on outcomes verified after the contracting horizon. Restricting compensation to an interim signal yields a strict effort wedge relative to the full-commitment benchmark. The key comparative static is that the wedge is largest when the long-horizon outcome would have been most informative if contractible; that is, a more informative noncontractible long-horizon outcome does not close the gap. We also quantify the shareholder value of extending the contracting horizon. The implication is that climate-linked CEO pay can address the tragedy of the horizon only when the relevant metrics are both informative and contractible.

Title: Never normal: Distributional properties of rare earth returns
Authors: Lidia Obojska, Ailie Charteris, Jan Jakub Szczygielski, Janusz Brzeszczyński
Abstract: Rare earth elements are critical to national economic security. However, the distributional properties of rare earth returns remain largely underexplored. We fit 81 distributions to 17 rare earth oxide (REO) return series using three goodness-of-fit criteria. Heavy-tailed distributions, including the Generalised Hyperbolic, Normal Inverse Gaussian, Cauchy, noncentral t, Student's t, and Generalised Error distributions, dominate, consistent with evidence from commodity markets, although some REO series exhibit more extreme tail behaviour. Some series also display asymmetry.
