These findings have implications for risk assessment, forecasting, volatility and connectedness modelling, as well as for the future pricing of REO derivatives, where standard frameworks may understate tail risk.

Title: Birth timing, stable population growth, and pay-as-you-go pensions
Abstract: This note studies a pure fertility-timing reform in a three-period OLG model. Holding completed fertility fixed, shifting births from middle age to youth raises the balanced-growth factor if N > 1 , lowers it if N < 1 , and leaves it unchanged if N = 1 . The same positive balanced-growth root λ determines cohort growth, the cohort ratio, and the steady-state PAYG support ratio λ 2 + λ . Thus the long-run support-ratio effect, and under an exogenous wage the pension-benefit effect, are positive in growing populations and negative in shrinking ones.

Title: Under the wing: The effect of parental proximity on intimate partner violence and underreporting
Abstract: Does proximity to the natal family protect women against intimate partner violence (IPV)? Leveraging Uzbekistan as a natural laboratory and an original list experiment among 835 married women, we find that women near their parents show a list-experiment prevalence estimate of 9.4% and no detectable reporting gap, whereas those far from their parents report only 8.5% in direct surveys, against a list-experiment estimate of 36.2%. Standard surveys do not merely undercount these victims — they invert the ranking of risk, making the most vulnerable women appear the safest. A parallel attitude experiment supports neither preference falsification nor cultural selection.

Title: Multiple monetary policy shocks from daily data: A heteroskedasticity IV approach
Abstract: We extend the heteroskedasticity IV estimator of Rigobon and Sack (2004) to multiple monetary policy shocks by imposing recursive zero restrictions on the impact matrix. Unlike high-frequency identification, the approach requires neither intraday tick data nor precise announcement timestamps, making it applicable to countries and historical periods where such data are unavailable. Applied to US FOMC announcements, we find causal effects similar to those of high-frequency identification. The heteroskedasticity-based instrument passes weak-instrument tests for the target shock, whereas results are mixed for high-frequency surprises. For the path shock, we obtain strong instruments for the majority of specifications and the underlying shock series is highly correlated with the high-frequency counterpart.

Title: Investment dynamics and monetary policy shocks: Evidence from EMU family firms
Authors: Paolo Canofari, Alessandro Piergallini, Matteo Renghini
Abstract: This paper examines family firms’ response to monetary policy tightening. By using a panel of about 130,000 non-listed EMU firms over the period 2011–2021, we show that family firms are more resilient to monetary policy shocks. Compared to non-family firms, they react to interest rate hikes by reducing tangible investments to a lesser extent. Fully family-controlled firms suffer a lower reduction in revenue and reallocate their debt from short to long term liabilities. Our results provide evidence of the existence of a corporate-ownership transmission channel. The presence of family firms appears to be an additional source of heterogeneity in response to monetary policy.

Title: Seconds of price discovery: Evidence from short-dated options
Abstract: Short-dated options may reveal stock-price information before stock quotes update. I test this using delta-bound violation events: consecutive option trade pairs whose empirical delta exceeds the upper Black–Scholes–Merton bound for calls or falls below the lower bound for puts. Among 77.44 million 2025 trade pairs, these events predict 0.23 basis points of same-direction stock movement over the next second. The result is positive in every month, survives matched controls and WRDS TAQ NBBO reconstruction, and aligns with inferred hedge pressure.

Title: Weekday bias in daily Google Trends spike detection
Abstract: Daily Google Trends data exhibit systematic day-of-week patterns that can contaminate spike detection in attention-based event studies. Applying a standard algorithm to raw data for 23 U.S. equities yields substantially more detected spikes than applying the same algorithm after weekday correction, with the excess concentrated on mid-week days. Validation against earnings announcements, SEC filings, and abnormal trading volume shows that weekday-corrected spikes align more closely with attention-relevant benchmarks than raw spikes. Researchers using daily Google Trends in threshold-based event studies should test for day-of-week seasonality and correct it when present.

Title: Single-step estimation of the partially linear model
Authors: Daniel J. Henderson, Nadine McCloud, Christopher F. Parmeter
Abstract: We consider a single-step approach to estimating the parametric coefficients and bandwidth parameters in a partially linear model. We establish a direct connection between this estimator and the two-step estimator of Robinson (1988). Simulations show that the resulting estimator improves recovery of the nonparametric component and the fitted conditional mean in most designs, while delivering coefficient estimates that are typically comparable to Robinson’s two-step estimator.

Title: The curse of sabotage - efficiency in an attacker - defender framework with gun & butter
Abstract: Standard economic rationale suggests that an enhancement of conflict-effort efficiency or sabotage efficiency in contests, benefits the player who is experiencing the improvement. This paper presents a model of sabotage in the context of attacker-defender contest with ‘gun’ and ‘butter’ (as posited by Chowdhury and Topolyan in 2026). We observe a strikingly counter-intuitive outcome – any increase in sabotage efficiency is counter-productive (even for the player experiencing the increase) in terms of equilibrium payoffs. The channel through which the result holds for both players (the attacker and the defender) is the shrinking size of the defender’s ‘butter’ when sabotage efficiency (of either player) increases. The paper also contradicts the findings of Chung in 2024 and Glökler, Pull and Stadler in 2022 who claim that endogenization of the prize alleviates or eliminates sabotage.

Title: The limits of leadership advantage in Stackelberg duopoly
Abstract: This paper studies how demand curvature limits first-mover advantage and shapes surplus division in a Stackelberg duopoly facing α[jls-end-space/]-concave demand for (Formula presented). Under constant symmetric marginal costs, I prove that across all possible equilibria, the leader-to-follower profit ratio is at least 1+5+4α2[jls-end-space/]. Thus, the leader is guaranteed to earn at least 61.8% more than the follower under log-concave demand (Formula presented) and at least twice as much under concave demand ((Formula presented) ). Under demand with decreasing marginal revenue ((Formula presented) ), the leadership advantage persists. I further derive a lower bound for the leader’s profit alongside an upper bound for deadweight loss. Extremal demand curves D for which Dα and (Formula presented) are affine attain all bounds for (Formula presented) .

Title: Upward pricing pressure in linked product and labor markets: Union bargaining and merger screens
Abstract: Setzler (2025) provides an important benchmark for merger analysis when firms exercise linked product-market and labor-market power under oligopoly and oligopsony. This note derives upward pricing pressure (UPP) screens for horizontal mergers under a different labor-market institution: unionization. In an efficient-bargaining model with Stone-Geary union utility, a price change that diverts sales to the merger partner may also affect that partner’s employment, wages, or workers’ outside options. Whereas product-labor links amplify merger harm in Setzler’s oligopsony benchmark, union-mediated effects can make product-side screens too lenient or too aggressive, thereby reversing whether a one-sided screen flags the merger.

Title: Procrastination traps and endogenous leadership in teams
Abstract: Teamwork can either cure or create procrastination. When present-biased teammates break a shared plan, the guilt of shirking depends on whether the partner acts too: shared inaction diffuses responsibility, while unilateral inaction betrays an acting partner. A team can therefore act when each member alone would delay, and stall when each alone would act. The harmful case is a coordination trap, arising only when both members are conditional starters who wait for each other. A single self-starter — one who acts whatever the partner does — breaks it, inducing exactly the outcome a committed visible leader would. A self-starter is an endogenous leader: heterogeneity in follow-through substitutes for leadership.

Title: Difference-in-differences with unit-specific trends: Bias in post-treatment estimates and a simple alternative
Abstract: Researchers often include unit-specific (e.g., state-specific) trends in difference-in-differences (DiD) specifications. Under standard DiD assumptions, these specifications still yield consistent estimates of dynamic treatment effects (i.e., separate effects for each post-treatment time period) but the pooled post-treatment coefficient is not consistent for the average treatment effect. This single coefficient is a weighted average of the dynamic coefficients, but some weights are often negative. This occurs even without a staggered rollout of treatment. Instead of estimating a pooled coefficient, researchers can estimate the average treatment effect as the mean of the dynamic effects.

Title: The gendered effects of rainfall shocks on stunting: evidence from Papua New Guinea
Authors: Jessica Leight, Rishabh Mukerjee, Emily Schmidt
Abstract: Rainfall fluctuations significantly reduce welfare for poor rural households in low- and middle-income countries dependent on rainfed agriculture for consumption, and the effects of these shocks can be borne disproportionately by vulnerable household members, particularly children and girls. We present new evidence around the effects of rainfall fluctuations on child anthropometric status in Papua New Guinea, an understudied context characterized by some of the highest stunting rates in the world. We show that negative fluctuations in rainfall within the first 12 months of life lead to a reduction in height-for-age and weight-for-age (though not stunting), but this effect is observed only for girls.

Title: The effect of master’s level social worker licensing reform in Illinois
Authors: Edward J. Timmons, Lawrence Han, Joshua Bandoch
Abstract: Shortages of healthcare professionals, particularly in mental health, remain an ongoing policy dilemma. Licensing requirements may be one potential factor contributing to this shortage. In 2022, Illinois eliminated the exam requirement for master’s level social workers (MSWs). Using data on the number of MSWs from several states, we estimate the effect of this policy change on the number of MSWs in Illinois using the synthetic control method. We find evidence that the elimination of the exam requirement increased the number of active MSW licenses in Illinois by approximately 2,600 licensees– a 50% increase. We also provide evidence that our estimates are both economically and statistically significant.

Title: How default risk shapes social choice
Authors: Wolfgang Höchtl, Rudolf Kerschbamer, Philipp Kircher, Sandra Ludwig, Alvaro Sandroni
Abstract: This paper reports the results of an experimental study investigating the role of uncertainty for pro-social behavior. We compare settings in which the decision-maker is solely responsible for the outcome to settings in which his choice is only implemented with some probability while with the complementary probability a “default” is implemented. We find that a sufficiently high probability of the default is necessary to alter decisions. Sufficiently-high-probability defaults lead to less giving by pro-social decision-makers, not only when the default is generous to the receiver but also when it is selfish. This violates monotonicity and is thus not consistent with expected utility theory nor with notions of ex ante fairness.

Title: Compatibility and investment incentives in dynamic procurement
Abstract: We study compatibility design in repeated procurement. A winning supplier can make a cost-reducing investment that carries over, while compatibility determines how much of the cost reduction is usable by the alternative supplier. Greater compatibility strengthens the alternative supplier but lowers the future value of winning and can weaken investment incentives. We show that when investment is sustainable, optimal compatibility is the lower of the unconstrained buyer-surplus optimum and the investment-sustaining ceiling. Except when zero compatibility is always optimal, buyer-optimal compatibility first rises and then falls with supplier patience.

Title: Large Language Model, trade threats and stock markets
Authors: Tian Yue, Zhixian Huang, Jiexiang Huang
Abstract: This study examines how politically driven trade-threat signals affect global equity markets. Using a Large Language Model (LLM), we construct a measure of trade-threat intensity from U.S. president Donald J. Trump’s posts on Truth Social and identify extreme threat events based on the upper tail of the score distribution. We find that these events are associated with significantly negative abnormal returns in global equity markets, concentrated within a short window around the event date. The effect exhibits substantial regional heterogeneity, with weaker responses in the Americas and stronger reactions in European, Asian, and Pacific markets. Our findings suggest that LLM-based measures of political communication capture economically meaningful signals associated with short-horizon movements in asset prices, highlighting the role of real-time political rhetoric in shaping global financial market dynamics.

Title: Doing good and doing well: A CAPM with complementary ESG and financial returns
Abstract: Empirical evidence shows that environmental, social, and governance (ESG) quality interacts with financial performance at the individual asset level: high-ESG firms outperform during crises and corporate social responsibility lowers systematic beta. Models with separable ESG preferences generate a greenium but no such interaction. We develop a capital asset pricing model (CAPM) with supermodular preferences over each asset’s return and ESG score. The equilibrium features an asset-specific denominator that compresses expected returns for high-ESG assets and generates a negative beta-ESG interaction, implying lower effective market sensitivity for green firms. We show that portfolio-level complementarity cannot produce this interaction, which yields a sharp test distinguishing our mechanism in the data. The model offers one rationalization of the beta-ESG interaction. We illustrate its quantitative content with four empirical studies.

Title: Investor fear, behavioural contagion, and the global dollar cycle: Evidence from BRICS currency markets
Abstract: We examine whether investor fear and anti-herding in BRICS currency markets spill over into the US dollar. Using Wavelet Coherence Analysis, we find that BRICS currencies exhibit systemic anti-herding behaviour that intensifies under financial stress. These behaviours transmit to the dollar, amplifying its volatility across short-, medium-, and long-term horizons. Our results challenge the conventional view of one-way risk transmission from advanced to emerging markets, showing instead that behavioural contagion from BRICS destabilises the reserve currency. This suggests that emerging-market investor behaviour may play a role in shaping global financial stability.

Title: Which demand elasticity should a monopoly use?
Abstract: Consider a non-durable goods monopolist who maximizes the present discounted value of profits. In steady state, which elasticity (short run or long run) should the monopolist use in the classic inverse-elasticity rule? Under some assumptions, the appropriate elasticity is a convex combination of the short-run and long-run elasticities of demand, where the weights depend upon the monopolist’s discount factor and the dynamics inherent in demand.

Title: Estimating exact efficiency in multi-weight spatial autoregressive stochastic frontier models
Abstract: Spatial autoregressive stochastic frontier models allow inefficiency to propagate across connected units. However, invertibility of the system matrix alone does not guarantee that exact spillover-corrected efficiency is admissible. If the inverse of the system matrix has negative entries, some non-negative inefficiency realizations imply negative total inefficiency and efficiency scores above one. Under non-negative spatial autoregressive parameters, we characterize the admissible parameter space for general non-negative spatial weighting matrices and extend the analysis to models with multiple weighting matrices. We also provide a practical sufficient condition and, for row-normalized multi-weight models, a simple necessary and sufficient restriction.

Title: Voice and distortion: When representatives misread the room
Abstract: A representative chooses policy on behalf of a group with heterogeneous preferences. Group members differ in voice (their salience to the representative). The representative maximizes perceived welfare based on a voice-weighted signal. The resulting policy distortion is proportional to the covariance between voice and preferences. When agents choose voice effort endogenously, equilibrium voice is U-shaped (quadratic in distance between preferences and policy). The equilibrium distortion is approximately one-third of a standard deviation times the skewness coefficient. It is non-zero only when the preference distribution is skewed. Combining the voice-weighted signal with a random sample can reduce the expected welfare loss.

Title: Economic growth with human, physical, and automation capital: The role of population decline
Authors: Subhrasil Chingri, Debasis Mondal, Klaus Prettner
Abstract: We examine the long-run economic consequences of population decline when automation and education respond endogenously to the demographic challenge. We show that, despite negative population growth, positive per capita output growth can be sustained. In equilibrium, output grows in line with physical and human capital accumulation, with household saving behavior playing a central role in sustaining growth. Moreover, the income share of raw labor declines, whereas the share of human capital remains constant.

Title: Correcting sample selection bias in PISA rankings
Abstract: This paper proposes a method to account for sample selection (survivor bias) in cross-country comparisons. International assessments such as the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) observe outcomes only for students enrolled in school at age 15, which can distort comparisons in countries with high dropout rates. I consider a quantile-based selection correction that delivers bounds on countries'average performance rather than point estimates. Using these bounds, I construct optimistic and pessimistic rankings, with each country's true rank lying between the two. An application to PISA 2018 shows that correcting for selection bias leads to substantial changes in countries'average scores and rankings.

Title: Is the distribution of resolvable uncertainty Type I extreme value? A test for random coefficient models using choice probabilities
Abstract: Probabilistic stated choices allow respondents to express uncertainty about their intended decisions. They are typically paired with random-coefficient models (RCM) that impose Type I extreme value (EV1) resolvable uncertainty. This paper proposes a test of these assumptions based on the restrictions imposed by the EV1 distribution on the population distribution of interquantile ranges of ex ante returns. Our test is rejected in four studies published in leading economics journals. In these applications, EV1-based estimators often perform reasonably well for median willingness-to-pay (WTP), but are less reliable for distributional objects such as the full WTP distribution.

Title: Central bank access and flight to safety
Authors: Lucia Gurrieri, Chase P. Ross, Ben Schmiedt, Alexandros P. Vardoulakis, Vladimir Yankov
Abstract: We examine whether access to the Federal Reserve's Overnight Reverse Repo Facility (ON RRP) affects money market fund flows during flight-to-safety episodes. We find that funds with ON RRP access serving sophisticated investors experience about a 1 percentage point increase in net daily flows over total assets during the March 2020 flight-to-safety episode relative to similar funds without access. The effect aligns with theoretical predictions and explains more than half of the inflows in those funds. Our results show that access to central bank deposit facilities amplifies flight-to-safety behavior.

Title: Asymmetric cost pass-through in gasoline retailing: The role of retailer size for pass-through
Abstract: Retail gasoline prices often adjust asymmetrically to cost shocks (“rockets and feathers”), but existing studies mostly use price data alone. Using daily station-level price and volume data from Sweden, we test whether asymmetry varies by station size. Nonlinear ARDL and error-correction models show that high-volume stations display more persistent short-run asymmetry, mainly due to slower adjustment after cost decreases. Weighting by station sales implies an annual consumer overcharge of about 1.25 billion SEK. Ignoring station heterogeneity biases aggregate loss estimates: using only low-volume stations understates losses, while using only high-volume stations overstates them.

Title: Extending the procedure of Engelberg et al. (2009) to surveys with unequal interval widths
Authors: Christoph K. Becker, Peter Duersch, Thomas Eife, Alexander Glas
Abstract: The approach by Engelberg et al. (2009) to convert probabilistic survey responses into continuous probability distributions implicitly assumes that the question intervals are equally wide. Almost all recently established surveys have intervals of unequal width. Applying the standard approach to these surveys gives implausible and potentially misleading results. This note shows how the approach of Engelberg et al. (2009) can be adjusted to account for intervals of unequal width.

Title: Investment timing and cash management with time-inconsistent preferences
Abstract: We develop a dynamic model of investment timing and liquidity management for a financially constrained all-equity firm whose entrepreneur has time-inconsistent preferences. We provide closed-form solutions for the equity value before and after investment and for the optimal investment threshold. We find that entrepreneur’s time inconsistency delays investment and increases the firm’s cash holdings for investment, which provides a potential theoretical explanation for why firms hold substantial cash. In addition, the investment financing mix violates the pecking order when the degree of time inconsistency is low: firms issue external equity even when internal funds are available. When the degree of time inconsistency is high, investment is financed entirely with internal cash, which aligns with the predictions of the pecking order.

Title: Supply chain risk perception, FinTech, and cross-regional capital flows: evidence from China
Authors: Zinan Wu, Wen Li, Xuesong Tang
Abstract: Using Chinese A-share listed firms from 2007 to 2022, this paper examines how supply chain risk perception affects cross-regional investment. We find that such perception significantly reduces cross-regional investment, while regional FinTech development mitigates this effect. Mechanism tests identify three channels: increased cash holdings, weakened risk-taking willingness, and strategic contraction. The inhibitory effect is more pronounced in firms within highly competitive industries, regions with lower internet development, and firms with severe managerial myopia. Our findings illuminate the spatial spillover effects of supply chain risk and offer evidence for optimizing cross-regional investment decisions.

Title: Does the climate challenge justify degrowth?
Authors: André Grimaud, Gilles Lafforgue, Luc Rouge
Abstract: Degrowth is often advocated as a response to the climate crisis, but its consistency with growth theory remains unclear. We develop an endogenous growth model of directed technical change and climate in which the economy relies on both a polluting fossil resource and a clean renewable alternative. We fully characterize the social optimum and show that accounting for climate damages may justify an initial phase of degrowth. Such a phase is more likely when fossil resources are abundant and fossil-oriented research is relatively inefficient. In all cases, long-run optimal growth remains positive.

Title: Population decline, capital deepening, and productivity: cross-country evidence
Abstract: This paper examines the relationship between population decline, capital deepening, and productivity growth using cross-country panel data over 1975–2023. Consistent with standard growth theory, slower population growth is associated with faster capital deepening. Conditional on controls, it is also linked to stronger GDP per worker growth, particularly in more technologically advanced economies. The results suggest that demographic headwinds can induce adjustment through capital deepening and labor-saving technologies. While population decline is not inherently beneficial, endogenous investment and technology responses partly offset its adverse effects on growth.

Title: Survival risk, the real interest rate, and the permanent income hypothesis in general equilibrium
Authors: Hao Li, Rongsheng Tang, Gaowang Wang
Abstract: Motivated by empirical evidence from cross-country panel regressions, we develop a heterogeneous-agent model with exponential utility to study how survival risk affects consumption, saving, and the equilibrium real interest rate. Survival risk increases impatience-induced dissaving demand, which raises the equilibrium interest rate through a higher demand for precautionary savings in general equilibrium. Although higher interest rates partially offset this effect by reducing dissaving demand, the overall impact of survival risk on the equilibrium interest rate remains positive. We further show that these results continue to hold under a more general recursive exponential utility specification.

Title: Corruption as a political control device: Enforceable vulnerability and coalition breakdown
Abstract: This paper develops a political economy model in which corruption enhances political control by generating enforceable vulnerability. We conceptualize corruption as a “hostage technology”: by allowing officials to accumulate incriminating evidence, the ruler ensures that elites remain strategically fragmented and vulnerable to selective punishment. We formalize this mechanism through a coordination game of political challenge and derive a risk-dominance threshold for coalition formation. A central theoretical result is the non-monotone effectiveness of enforcement: while moderate enforcement deters political challenges, excessively strong enforcement can paradoxically undermine political control by eliminating the very leverage — incriminating evidence — needed to discipline elites. The model yields sharp comparative statics linking tolerated corruption, enforcement capacity, monitoring technology, and political threat, providing a unified theoretical explanation for the coexistence of systemic corruption and durable political stability.

Title: Post-disaster aid and development of the manufacturing sector: Lessons from a natural experiment in China revisited
Abstract: Bulte et al. (2018), examining the effects of the 2008 earthquake in China, report quasi-experimental evidence of Dutch Disease dynamics in the context of post-disaster aid and recovery. The authors’ conclusion from the synthetic control analysis relies exclusively on visual inspection of the post-earthquake gap between the treated unit and its synthetic control, without implementing the method’s formal inferential procedures. Our reanalysis shows that, while the gap may appear visually large and persistent over time, it is not statistically significant. Within the synthetic control framework, we find no evidence supporting aid-induced Dutch Disease dynamics. This weakens the original study’s conclusion by showing that the reported effect is not robust to alternative methods.

Title: Accounting for structural breaks in the Hamilton filter
Abstract: This paper reveals that the regression-based trend-cycle decomposition of Hamilton (2018) introduces spurious cyclical dynamics when time series undergo structural breaks. Because the filter relies on an h[jls-end-space/]-step ahead projection, trend adjustment mechanically lags behind regime shifts, inducing large and persistent biases in the cyclical component. We propose a parsimonious modification using a dummy-variable structure that allows the regression intercept and autoregressive components to adjust to identified breaks. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations show that this approach substantially reduces Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) across a wide range of data-generating processes. These gains are robust to variations in break magnitude, timing and number; sample size; and signal-to-noise ratio. Notably, our approach remains superior in pseudo-real-time settings, where the benefits from break-adjustment outweigh the costs of recursive break date estimation and revision. An empirical application to the Swiss franc/euro exchange rate demonstrates that our modification avoids the spurious cyclical spikes generated by standard filters during major policy shifts. Both ex-post and recursive real-time estimates confirm that our proposed framework provides a more reliable decomposition for macroeconomic assessment and inference.

Title: Do taxpayer assistance programs improve compliance among small firms? Evidence from Brazil
Authors: Simone Covre, Paulo Henrique Muller Prado, Enlinson Mattos
Abstract: This paper examines the effects of taxpayer assistance on corporate tax compliance using administrative data from Brazil’s simplified tax regime (Simples Nacional). Exploiting two large-scale assistance campaigns implemented at different points in time, we adopt a difference-in-differences design, using firms treated later as a control group. We find that assistance generates a large and statistically significant short-run increase in reported tax liabilities: reported amounts rise by 41 percent on average, with peak effects exceeding 270 percent within three months, driven by adjustment tax liabilities. However, these effects are temporary and dissipate within fifteen months. Firms exposed to repeated interventions respond more strongly, suggesting reinforcement effects.

Title: An upwind scheme for continuous-time optimization with two endogenous state variables
Abstract: I develop a novel upwind scheme to solve the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) equation with two endogenous state variables. The algorithm chooses the upwind direction that gives the largest Hamiltonian to numerically determine optimal policies over the full state space. The choice of upwind direction in each iteration is intuitive, and can be implemented without splitting asset drifts into multiple components. I compare optimal policy functions on a wealth grid produced by the upwind scheme with those obtained from the splitting scheme used in the literature, and find discrepancies of policy functions at the boundaries.

Title: Climate and sovereign default risk
Abstract: Does climate risk necessarily raise sovereign default risk? While a growing literature documents adverse effects from realized disasters, the implications of long-term (chronic) climate risk remain unclear. Using an endogenous default model with climate shocks, we isolate chronic physical risk from acute disaster realizations. We show that higher climate risk can increase sovereign bond prices by reducing default incentives. Risk-averse governments value continued market access as insurance against future shocks, strengthening repayment motives. While acute disasters still depress prices on impact, chronic risk can operate through a precautionary channel.

Title: State-dependent within-artist anchor reversal in ultra-contemporary art auctions
Abstract: In a panel of 4259 ultra-contemporary auction lots (39 artists, 130 houses, 2005Q4–2026Q1), |log(hammer/high estimate)| compresses with within-artist rank only for artists with above-median dispersion in their first five lots (TWFE β = −0.293, wild cluster bootstrap p = 0.015). Of 19 such imprecise-start artists, 18 begin above estimate (Fisher exact p = 0.0008 vs the empirical sample marginal). The compression is not a floor effect: a precise-start subgroup with mean |gap| = 0.456 — well above the imprecise group's terminal level — shows no convergence (β = −0.025, p = 0.883). The compression operates on hammer prices, not on specialist estimate widths.

Title: Financial literacy, financial vulnerability, and buy now, pay later use
Abstract: Using data from the 2024 U.S. National Financial Capability Study, this paper examines the association between financial literacy and buy now, pay later (BNPL) use. A simple framework predicts that greater financial literacy is associated with lower BNPL use, but this link weakens when financial constraints bind. Consistent with this prediction, we find an overall negative association between financial literacy and BNPL use. That pattern, however, is concentrated among non-vulnerable households and becomes weaker, disappears, or reverses under financial vulnerability.

Title: Impact of legalization of recreational marijuana on drug law violations: Evidence from US colleges and universities
Abstract: The use of various controlled and illegal substances, especially by young adults, has been a cause of much concern among policymakers, law enforcement officials, educators, and parents. State-level legalization of recreational marijuana in the United States raised concerns about potential adverse impacts on campus drug use and drug law violations. This paper combines data from three sources for 2001-02 to 2023-24, including college campus drug law violations that are collected under the Clery Act of 1990. We find that state legalization of recreational marijuana substantially reduced the arrests and disciplinary incidents for drug law violations.

Title: Paying for parity: Incentivizing men in feminized occupations
Authors: Lucía Cobreros, Carlos Sunyer, Judit Vall Castelló
Abstract: We find that gender-neutral financial incentives increased the share of male General Practice (GP) residents by 30% in Catalonia, Spain. Exploiting a salary supplement policy for GP residents and a synthetic difference-in-differences design, we estimate an increase of 8.3 percentage points, with effects concentrated in areas receiving larger wage increases. We also document suggestive evidence of lower GP vacancy rates in treated regions after the policy, although this pattern cannot be interpreted causally. To our knowledge, these results provide the first causal evidence that gender-neutral financial incentives can attract men into a highly feminized occupation.

Title: Economic mobility beliefs and parental investment: Experimental evidence
Authors: Rebecca Ryan, Ariel Kalil, Marlis M. Schneider, Mesmin Destin, David Silverman, Ivan A. Hernandez
Abstract: Economic theory predicts that parents invest more in children when expected returns are higher. (cid:55)(cid:75)(cid:72)(cid:3) (cid:68)(cid:88)(cid:87)(cid:75)(cid:82)(cid:85)(cid:86) test whether beliefs about societal economic mobility affect these expectations and subsequent

Title: Net worth trap under ambiguity
Authors: Bangru Shi, Yaoyao Wu, Siqi Zhao
Abstract: We develop a macro model with financial frictions where high-productivity farmers must rent land and face ambiguity about production. Ambiguity makes land demand state dependent: it is pro-cyclical when farmers fear low expected returns and counter-cyclical when they anticipate higher future rental costs. Pro-cyclical demand compresses production in downturns and yields competing effects on the net-worth trap. With moderate ambiguity aversion, farmers cut land use, lowering endogenous risk and avoiding the trap. With strong aversion, it slows net-worth rebuilding, leading to sluggish recoveries and economic vulnerability.

Title: News on asymmetric fiscal multipliers
Abstract: This paper investigates the asymmetric effects of expansionary and contractionary fiscal shocks in the U.S. economy using a state-of-the-art non-linear local projection framework. To identify fiscal shocks, I use a proxy based on revisions to the mean forecast of government spending growth from the Survey of Professional Forecasters, which represent unexpected changes in expectations about government spending. The estimated fiscal multipliers are larger following positive fiscal shocks than following negative ones, indicating asymmetric effects of fiscal policy interventions.

Title: Austria one century apart: Persistent effects of hyperinflation on inflation expectations
Abstract: Can the memory of past inflation shape how people form expectations about prices today? Using regional inflation data from Austria’s 1921–22 hyperinflation linked to quarterly consumer surveys (May 2020–Oct 2024), we document a persistent association between historical inflation exposure and contemporary inflation expectations: individuals from regions more exposed to the historical episode report higher inflation expectations a century later. We further show that regional newspapers in historically high-inflation areas devote greater attention to inflation, suggesting local media environments contribute to the intergenerational transmission of inflation attitudes. The collective memory of major inflation episodes can durably shape expectation formation.

Title: Unfiltered consumption and the elasticity of intertemporal substitution
Abstract: This paper estimates the elasticity of intertemporal substitution (EIS) from the aggregate consumption Euler equation using Kroencke’s (2017) unfiltered consumption data. Unlike the published NIPA series used in most studies, unfiltered consumption is designed to recover the latent series obscured by statistical smoothing. Using weak-instrument-robust GMM inference, we show that this measurement choice matters for EIS estimation. With conventional filtered consumption, confidence sets typically include zero and are often uninformative. With unfiltered consumption, confidence sets exclude zero and provide a positive lower bound. The near-zero EIS estimates in the literature may partly reflect a measurement artifact rather than household preferences.

Title: Oil supply shocks and inflation tail risks
Authors: Andrea De Polis, Álvaro Fernández-Gallardo, José Nicolás Rosas
Abstract: We analyze the asymmetric transmission of oil supply news shocks to the inflation distribution in the United States, the euro area, and the United Kingdom. Using quantile local projections and high-frequency identification, we document a stark asymmetry across these three large advanced economies: while median responses are transitory, the 90th quantile exhibits significant and persistent increases beyond one year. This upside tail sensitivity, consistent with state-dependent pricing, suggests that supply shocks are structural innovations to the skewness of the inflation distribution. Monetary policy should actively monitor such persistent inflation tail risks to keep expectations anchored.

Title: Efficiency in producing life satisfaction: A stochastic frontier analysis
Authors: Gang Chen, Puguang Nie, Xibin Zhang
Abstract: We employ a semiparametric stochastic frontier model with ordinal outcomes to study efficiency in producing overall life satisfaction. Inefficiency is specified as an unknown function of discrete characteristics using a nonparametric Nadaraya–Watson estimator. A Bayesian procedure is developed to estimate latent variables and model parameters, including the bandwidths of the nonparametric component. The empirical analysis examines the role of the Big Five personality traits and individual resilience, showing that individuals who are more extraverted, agreeable, conscientious, and resilient, or less neurotic, tend to be more efficient in converting satisfaction across multiple life domains into overall life satisfaction.

Title: On the existence of equilibrium in the super manager model
Authors: Kailin Ding, Zhenyu Cui, Yanchu Liu, Cai Kure Wu
Abstract: The super manager model developed in Baranchuk et al. (2011) is revisited in this paper. We show that an important condition required for the firm’s optimization problem was overlooked. Once this condition is imposed, the market equilibrium derived in the original paper may fail to exist for certain parameter values. In particular, the existence of interior hierarchical equilibrium is conditional on managerial productivity exceeding organizational costs, and disappears when demand is sufficiently weak, in the sense that no admissible interior super-manager equilibrium existsWe derive the corrected equilibrium system and provide numerical illustrations showing that sufficiently weak demand can eliminate any admissible interior super-manager equilibrium. Our results not only clarify the conditions under which the equilibrium of the super manager model is well defined, but also provide economic interpretations when no admissible interior super-manager equilibrium exists.

Title: Non-fundamental price pressure and the pass-through to mortgage rates
Abstract: We show that non-fundamental price pressure in sovereign bond markets can raise household borrowing costs even when it lowers benchmark yields. Using recommendations of a Chilean advisory firm as an identified shock to government bonds—the mortgage pricing benchmark—buying-pressure events lower yields yet widen spreads by more than the decline, raising mortgage rates on net. Lenders retain the compression as a wider margin, leaving borrowers worse off. Selling pressure raises yields, with mortgage rates partially tracking at longer horizons. Two placebo exercises confirm the results. Price pressure that compresses benchmark yields can leave household borrowing costs higher, not lower.

Title: Mispredictions about dishonesty after unfair treatment
Abstract: We used a preregistered incentivized online experiment to examine whether unfair treatment increases dishonesty toward uninvolved third parties and whether observers anticipate such effects. Unfairly treated participants were not significantly more likely to lie for personal gain. In contrast, spectators were nearly twice as likely to bet that unfairly treated participants would lie and judged such lying as more morally acceptable following unfair treatment. These patterns provide preliminary evidence of a sizeable belief–behavior gap in expectations about how unfairness influences dishonesty.

Title: Moral hazard spillovers across losses
Abstract: This note analyzes how the moral hazard underlying one loss spills over to another. In a competitive insurance market with two mutually exclusive losses — one is subject to moral hazard while the other is not — we demonstrate that policyholders buy only partial insurance coverage for both losses, even if the second is free of moral hazard. Moreover, the coverage for the second loss is always more generous, and numerical analysis shows that the coverage gap widens with more efficient prevention efforts or lower risk aversion. A mutual assistance mechanism that allows acquainted policyholders to share uninsured risks is introduced to alleviate moral hazard and enhance social welfare.

Title: Renegotiation and heterogeneous beliefs with risk neutrality
Abstract: I study a risk-neutral principal–agent model with moral hazard, limited liability, and renegotiation. With common beliefs, renegotiation is irrelevant under risk neutrality. With heterogeneous beliefs, renegotiation reshapes the contract into a pure “side bet”: after the action is sunk, the principal concentrates all promised compensation on the outcome the agent overweights the most, which can raise compensation costs and even make some actions non-implementable. Under the monotone-likelihood-ratio property and optimism (likelihood-ratio dominance), the disagreement-maximizing outcome coincides with the incentive-efficient outcome, so renegotiation is again innocuous.

Title: Corrigendum to “Country-level cryptocurrency uncertainty and bank cost of capital” [Economics Letters, 256, October 2025, 112614]
Authors: Abu Hanifa Md. Noman, Mohammad Abdullah, Larisa Yarovaya

Title: Bayesian group shrinkage for spatial autoregressive model with convex combination of spatial weights matrices
Authors: Zhengzheng Cai, Xiaoyi Han, Jianchao Zhuo
Abstract: This paper investigates the spatial autoregressive model with convex combination of spatial weights matrices categorized in groups, an empirically relevant specification that has received limited attention in the spatial econometrics literature. We employ the Group Inverse-Gamma Gamma (GIGG) prior introduced by Boss et al. (2024) to distinguish between relevant and irrelevant groups, identify influential spatial weights matrices, and mitigate multicollinearity arising from correlations among matrices within the same group. A computationally efficient Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm is developed for estimation, inference, and hyperparameter tuning. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed prior performs effectively in both parameter estimation and variable selection.

Title: The SNAP benefit cycle beyond the mean: Substitution across payment sources and distributional heterogeneity
Abstract: Mean grocery spending by Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) households peaks at benefit receipt and declines thereafter. Using novel shopping receipt data with observed trip-level tender information across a range of retailers, store formats, and shopping channels, we examine whether households partially smooth grocery spending over the benefit cycle through substitution across payment sources and whether the effects of benefit receipt vary across the grocery spending distribution. We find evidence of smoothing at the extensive margin through modest increases in non-SNAP-funded shopping trips. Distributional analyses reveal more pronounced spending cycles at higher grocery spending quantiles along with suggestive evidence of weaker substitution toward non-SNAP-funded payment sources.

Title: The fragility of the partisan inflation gap: Evidence from the United Kingdom
Abstract: Partisan theory predicts that left-leaning governments tolerate higher inflation, and UK data appear to confirm it. Before 1997, inflation averaged three percentage points higher under Labour than the Conservatives. I show this gap is not robust. It is the product of a single Labour government (1974–79) that coincided with the OPEC oil shocks; a randomisation test at the level of governments returns (Formula presented), and omitting any one of nine governments can swing the gap by up to four points. With so few in the sample, the data cannot sustain the partisan effect they appear to show.

Title: Obviously strategy-proof choice of social acts
Abstract: We study obviously strategy-proof implementation in the framework of social choice over acts introduced by Bahel and Sprumont (2020). We characterize the class of unanimous social choice functions that are implementable via obviously strategy-proof mechanisms. Our main result shows that a unanimous social choice function is obviously strategy-proof implementable if and only if it is dictatorial.

Title: Nonverbal signals and market uncertainty: Evidence from bank of japan press conferences
Abstract: This paper examines the within-conference relationship between nonverbal features of the Bank of Japan governor and post-answer realized volatility of Japanese Government Bond futures. Using 1,557 question-and-answer segments from 79 post-meeting press conferences during 2016-2026, I regress realized volatility of Japanese Government Bond futures on principal component indices of facial and audio features extracted from conference videos. Facial indicators exhibit a significant positive association with volatility, even after controlling for verbal policy stance, policy surprises, and governor fixed effects. The short-horizon correlation is preserved under a censored-RV robustness check that addresses overlap with subsequent answers, while longer windows attenuate.

Title: Measuring climate ambition: Annualization and ranking discrepancy
Abstract: Corporate climate mitigation targets are increasingly relevant, but ambition measurement remains inconsistent. Linear annual reduction (LAR) and compound annual reduction (CAR) are common measures of climate ambition, but they imply different reduction paths and may reverse ambition rankings when percentage reductions and target horizons differ. I derive the exact pairwise ranking-reversal condition, revealing that LAR favors shorter, shallower targets compared to CAR, and apply this framework to the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) Target Dashboard. The results confirm substantial ranking reversal depending on whether LAR or CAR is used to define ambition.

Title: Short-term reversal persists globally—If properly measured
Abstract: Short-term reversal appears to have weakened in international equity markets because standard measures mix firm-specific and industry-wide returns. When evaluated relative to industry peers, the reversal persists. Using data from 64 countries, the conventional strategy delivers negligible returns, whereas an industry-adjusted strategy earns 0.53% per month with a Sharpe ratio of 0.74. The effect reflects the reversal of firm-specific shocks masked by persistent industry components. A regret-based signal captures the same industry-relative variation, adding no incremental return. Reversal did not disappear; it was mismeasured.

Title: Partisan differences among independents: Evidence from household economic expectations
Abstract: I document that self-declared politically Independent households with partisan leanings change economic expectations in ways that resemble weak partisans. Republican leaners align more with weak Republicans, while Democratic leaners are similar to weak Democrats in their macroeconomic beliefs. This insight has important implications for survey design and for how researchers categorize political affiliation in economic analyses. Classifying leaners as neutral Independents can distort estimates of partisan differences.

Title: Editorial Board
Corrigendum to “Student beauty and grades under in-person and remote teaching” [Economics Letters 2019 (2022) 110782]
Abstract: The authors regret a typo in the text. The sentence “Concomitantly, there is no significant relationship between attractiveness and grades for the non-quantitative courses” should be replaced by “Concomitantly, there is no significant relationship between attractiveness and grades for the quantitative courses.” The authors would like to apologise for any inconvenience caused.

Title: Comparing unemployment-based recession indicators
Abstract: This paper evaluates modifications to the standard insured unemployment rate (IUR) as recession indicators. We replace the lagged covered employment denominator with a more timely employment measure and construct an alternative indicator based on initial claims. These alternatives often signal recessions earlier than the standard IUR, especially in post-1971 business cycles. We also digitize historical unemployment insurance data to extend the IUR series back to 1947, allowing evaluation over a broader set of recessions.

Title: Price discovery in cryptocurrency markets: sub-second evidence
Abstract: Using transaction-level data for leading digital assets traded on the largest cryptocurrency exchange, we examine trading activity at the 100-millisecond horizon. A disproportionally high trading activity is found during the first 100 milliseconds of a given second in both spot market and perpetual futures. We consider two competing explanations rooted in exchange-level infrastructure versus participant-driven algorithmic trading. Trades executed during the first 100 milliseconds of a second have a significant contribution to permanent price changes after adjusting for the elevated trading intensity during that interval, which is consistent with the notion of algorithmic trading and its leading role in price discovery in the cryptocurrency markets.

Title: Cryptokurtosis: Frequent trading fuels higher losses
Authors: Stavros Degiannakis, George Filis, Grigorios Siourounis
Abstract: We assess the impact of cryptocurrencies ultra-high frequency trading on financial stability. Focusing on three well-established cryptocurrencies, namely Bitcoin, Ethereum and Sui, we show that as the trading frequency increases, so do the excess potential losses of the investors, over and above the anticipated losses based on the Value-at-Risk. This is led by the exponential growth of the kurtosis that is exhibited at high-frequency trading. Given that currently the minimum capital requirements do not differentiate between the trading frequency but only between the type of cryptoassets groups, we show that such overlook poses a threat to the financial stability.

Title: Oil on the water: How shipping cost pressures shape the inflationary effects of oil shocks
Abstract: This paper investigates the impact of shipping cost pressures on the transmission of oil supply shocks to inflation. Using local projections on a panel of oil-importing and exporting countries, we show that headline, energy, and producer price inflation respond more strongly and persistently to oil supply shocks when shipping cost pressures are high. While the responses of importers and exporters typically differ, high shipping cost pressures are associated with stronger inflationary effects of oil shocks in both sets of countries. These findings extend to the case of oil demand shocks.

Title: Habit formation and endogenous business cycle
Abstract: This paper examines the conditions and mechanisms through which habit formation can generate endogenous business cycles. We integrate habit formation into two canonical preference specifications—multiplicative and additive habits—and show that a period-2 cycle emerges under the multiplicative specification, but not under the additive one. These cyclical dynamics are driven by distant complementarity and the coefficient of relative risk aversion. Within the multiplicative framework, we also derive separate necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of such cycles.

Title: “Trade uncertainty and export market penetration in newly industrializing countries”
Authors: Salih Yildirim, Ecem Ozkan, Ibrahim Ethem Akyildiz
Abstract: Using panel data for nine newly industrializing countries (NICs) from 2000 to 2022, this paper examines the effect of trade uncertainty on export market penetration using the CS-ARDL method. Using panel data for nine newly industrializing countries (NICs) from 2000 to 2022, this paper examines the effect of trade uncertainty on export market penetration using the CS-ARDL method. The findings show that trade uncertainty associated with reducing export market penetration in the long run. Tariff-related entry costs are also negatively related to export market penetration, suggesting that entry frictions reinforce the adverse effects of uncertainty on the extensive margin of trade. Robustness checks using trade policy uncertainty and container port traffic confirm the main results.

Title: Fiscal demographic reversal
Abstract: We study how rising longevity affects the long-run real interest rate in an overlapping-generations model with mortality risk and accidental bequests to the young. Longer lives increase retirement saving, which tends to lower the interest rate, but they also reduce such bequests and shift asset payoffs from young savers to surviving retirees, weakening aggregate saving. Public debt amplifies this second force. When debt is sufficiently high, further increases in longevity eventually raise the steady-state interest rate. Thus, longevity need not continue to depress interest rates: with large public debt, the relationship between longevity and the interest rate becomes non-monotonic.

Title: Do entrepreneurs stay in their industry? Evidence from population-wide data
Abstract: Using population-wide administrative data, we study industry persistence in career transitions, focusing on entrepreneurial entry. We document that individuals who enter entrepreneurship are significantly more likely to remain in the same industry as in their prior employment compared to individuals who change workplace but remain in paid employment. This persistence is particularly strong among individuals with longer prior industry experience. We further show that entrepreneurs who remain in their prior industry have higher post-entry incomes and income growth than those who switch industries. The results suggest that entrepreneurship largely reflects industry-specific career continuation rather than broad occupational reallocation.

Title: Estimation of functional coefficient panel data models with endogenous selectivity and fixed effects: A pairwise approach
Authors: Daniel J. Henderson, Juan M. Rodriguez-Poo, Alexandra Soberon, Taining Wang
Abstract: This paper develops a complementary estimation approach for functional coefficient panel data models with sample selection and fixed effects. We propose a pairwise differencing strategy that avoids imposing restrictions on the fixed effects at the cost of not directly estimating level coefficients on time-invariant regressors. We derive the estimator’s asymptotic properties and show via simulations that it performs competitively relative to existing methods. Eliminating the need to estimate individual fixed effects yields considerable computational savings, making the approach suitable for large datasets.

Title: Mandatory vs. voluntary disclosure of product risk information: The roles of observability, product liability, and product-risk correlation
Abstract: We compare incentives to acquire product-risk information under Cournot competition with product liability and correlated risks. Disclosure regimes are indexed by the probability that acquired information is discretionary rather than compulsory, so mandatory and voluntary disclosure are polar cases. Strategic concealment creates an opacity feedback: when acquisition effort is observable, higher effort changes how the market interprets silence. This can reduce acquisition incentives and overturn the standard acquisition-incentive ranking. We also identify a neutrality locus where market beliefs are payoff-irrelevant and acquisition incentives reflect only the output-adjustment value of information.

Title: Rounding error and misallocation
Authors: Jing Hang, Di Lu, Wenbiao Sha
Abstract: Measurement error poses a challenge to measuring misallocation. Using Chinese manufacturing data (1998–2007), we exploit rounding — a directly observable form of measurement error — in firms’ reported labor, capital, and value added. The share of values ending in zero exceeds 20% for each variable, more than double the 10% uniform benchmark. Within industry-year cells, the standard deviation of log labor productivity is 0.021 higher among firms whose reports end in zero than among firms ending in other non-rounding digits, with a sharply larger differential in small-firm industries. At the aggregate level, including rounded observations lowers estimated allocative efficiency by 1.6 percentage points.

Title: The cost of cross-border listing: Evidence from the Holding Foreign Companies Accountable Act
Authors: Renhui Fu, Fang Gao, Yanhui Wang, Huimin Zhou
Abstract: In 2020, the U.S. enacted the Holding Foreign Companies Accountable Act (HFCAA), requiring U.S.-listed foreign firms to submit audit working papers and verify the absence of government control, with delisting as a penalty for noncompliance. Using an event study approach, we document significantly negative stock market reactions to HFCAA legislative events among U.S.-listed Chinese firms. The effects are more pronounced for data-sensitive firms and state-owned enterprises, as well as for firms listed only in the United States and those facing larger financing constraints. Overall, our findings show that cross-border listing can impose significant regulatory costs stemming from cross-border enforcement frictions.

Title: Random-weighting bootstrap correction for Granger causality tests in VAR models with time-varying variance of unknown form
Abstract: In this paper, we study Granger causality testing in vector autoregressive (VAR) models with time-varying variance of unknown form, where the conventional Wald statistic converges to a weighted sum of chi-squared distributions and can induce substantial size distortions. To address this issue, we propose a random-weighting bootstrap correction, and Monte Carlo simulations show that it attains rejection frequencies close to the nominal level under time-varying variance while maintaining competitive power in finite samples.

Title: Product differentiation, economies of scale and entry
Abstract: This paper extends the standard circular city model of spatial competition to incorporate economies of scale. We demonstrate that new market entry generates a negative externality by fragmenting demand and forcing existing firms to operate at a less efficient scale. This scale-fragmentation channel widens the wedge between private and social entry incentives, leading to an amplified excess-entry result. When firms can endogenously invest to lower their unit costs, market entry remains socially excessive.

Title: Estimation of heterogeneous spatial panel data models with multiple structural breaks and a multifactor error structure
Authors: Siqi Dai, Wenting Wang, Chaowen Zheng
Abstract: This study considers heterogeneous spatial panel data models with multifactor errors and multiple unknown structural breaks in unit-specific coefficients. To address the dual challenges of endogeneity and heterogeneity across both time and cross-sectional units, we first eliminate factor dependence using a robust common correlated effects approach that relies exclusively on cross-sectional averages of the regressors, an approach we term CCEX. Multiple structural breakpoints are then estimated by the simultaneous estimation procedure of Bai and Perron (1998). We also propose a sequential test to determine the number of breaks. Within each identified regime, heterogeneous parameters are estimated by integrating CCEX with instrumental variables techniques. The proposed method yields consistent estimation for number of breaks, break dates and structural parameters, with Monte Carlo simulations demonstrating its superior finite-sample performance.

Title: When to front-load persuasion
Abstract: When receivers process persuasive messages coarsely, timing matters even when content is fixed. In a two-period competitive game, greater belief stickiness shifts equilibrium timing from back-loading to spreading, then to mixing, and finally to front-loading. Under budget asymmetry, the larger sender’s extra message lengthens the spreading region. With an initial lead, timing instead turns on a single threshold from mutual delay to asymmetric mixed play with early attack. Stickier beliefs make early leads more durable, increasing the value of preemption relative to delay, unlike in the Bayesian benchmark.

Title: Gender gap in pension literacy: Evidence from Italy
Authors: Barbara Alemanni, Umberto Filotto, Gennaro De Novellis, Gian Paolo Stella
Abstract: This paper examines gender differences in pension literacy in Italy, distinguishing between knowledge of the public pension pillar and knowledge of supplementary pensions. Using a cross-sectional survey of 2436 working-age adults, we document a substantial raw gender gap in pension literacy. Once observable differences between men and women are taken into account, these characteristics explain roughly half of the gap, while the remaining half persists even after conditioning on observables. Our findings further show that the gender gap is not uniform across pension domains. Women remain significantly less informed about the public pension system, whereas the gap disappears in the case of supplementary pensions. These results suggest that women’s lower pension literacy reflects not only broader differences in financial literacy, but also a specific disadvantage in understanding the public pension system.

Title: Non-linear transmission of benchmark rates to aircraft lease pricing
Abstract: Aircraft leasing is a central mechanism through which airlines expand fleet capacity. This study examines how changes in the Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR) relate to aircraft lease pricing and whether this relationship varies across interest rate levels. Using generalized additive models and piecewise regression, we reveal the nonlinear relationships between SOFR and lease rates and how they differ with aircraft age. The linkage is strongest in low-interest rates. When financing costs are high, the negative effect of aircraft age is reduced, resulting in narrower lease-rate differentials between newer and older aircraft. These findings provide new insights into the interaction between benchmark funding costs and lease rates.

Title: Endogenous volatility and strategic disclosure in mutual funds
Abstract: We develop an information design model where mutual fund managers jointly choose portfolio volatility and disclosure policy to maximize fee revenue from risk-averse investors. We demonstrate that persuasion fundamentally drives risk-taking. When high risk-free rates render funds unappealing, managers endogenously inflate asset volatility to manufacture the information asymmetry required to persuade investors. Optimal volatility strictly increases with the risk-free rate and decreases with investor risk aversion. Our framework highlights how high interest rates inadvertently incentivize excessive risk-taking in asset management.

Title: Green acquisitions
Abstract: Prior research suggests that investors value green firms at a premium. We add to this line of research and show that the acquirer’s cumulative abnormal return after the announcement of an acquisition is increasing in the “greenness” of the target. We find tentative evidence suggesting that this pattern is more pronounced after the 2015 Paris agreement, and is more pronounced for the first acquisition of a green target by the same acquirer.

Title: Blockchain adoption and corporate investment efficiency: Evidence from the blockchain-based electronic invoice system
Authors: Junjie Yang, Liwen Wang, Jing Ma
Abstract: This paper examines how blockchain adoption affects corporate investment efficiency in China. Exploiting the staggered regional rollout of China's blockchain-based electronic invoice system as a quasi-natural experiment, we employ a difference-in-differences design and find that blockchain adoption significantly improves corporate investment efficiency. The results remain robust across a series of endogeneity and robustness tests. Mechanism analysis indicates that the effect operates primarily through improvements in financial reporting quality. Overall, our findings provide novel causal evidence on the real economic consequences of blockchain adoption and highlight the role of government-mandated information technology infrastructure in enhancing firms' resource allocation efficiency.

Title: Capital-biased tax incentives and labor market power: Evidence from China
Authors: Lishuang Huang, Chang Liu, Xunchang Zhang
Abstract: This paper identifies the causal effect of capital-biased tax incentives on labor market power by analyzing China’s 2004 value-added tax pilot reform, which enabled firms to deduct investment in production capital. We utilize firm-level administrative data to estimate production functions and compute wage markdowns. Our difference-in-differences analysis reveals that the reform increased labor market power by approximately 6.1%, largely through a labor-saving growth channel without a comparable increase in wages. The effect is more pronounced among firms that are already better positioned to take advantage of cheaper production capital.

Title: Can public works increase caste-based conflicts? Evidence from India’s National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme
Authors: Shampa Bhattacharjee, Agrani Gupta, Radhani Jagadish Kumar, Arka Roy Chaudhuri
Abstract: This paper studies whether the world’s largest workfare scheme reduces targeted violence against marginalized groups. Leveraging the district-wise phased rollout of the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (MGNREGS), we employ a difference-in-differences design to identify the causal impact of MGNREGS implementation on targeted crimes against disadvantaged caste groups. Our findings show a significant increase in reported caste-based crimes following the scheme’s introduction. We discuss and provide suggestive evidence on the mechanisms.

Title: Multi-prize contests under dual utility
Authors: Shanglyu Deng, Ruiqi Li, Zenan Wu
Abstract: We analyze multi-prize nested Tullock contests with symmetric players and characterize the effort-maximizing prize allocation under Yaari’s (1987) dual theory. Our analysis yields several key results: (i) risk aversion tends to disincentivize effort in concentrated (top-heavy) prize structures; (ii) the optimal prize structure consistently features an egalitarian distribution, wherein prizes are allocated equally among winners; and (iii) the optimal number of prizes is non-decreasing in the degree of risk aversion. For sufficiently risk-averse players, it is optimal to award equal prizes to all but one participant.

Title: Persistence, patience and costly information acquisition
Abstract: A forward-looking agent observes signals of a state that follows a Gaussian AR(1) process. He balances the cost of having imprecise beliefs with the cost of acquiring more precise signals. I characterize his optimal information acquisition policy, and analyze how his steady-state beliefs and costs depend on persistence (the AR(1) parameter) and patience (the agent's discount factor). Higher persistence has a non-monotone effect on belief precision and raises overall costs. Higher patience makes beliefs more precise and lowers overall costs.

Title: The economic cost of selection neglect in portfolio choice: evidence from Australian fine wine auctions
Abstract: We estimate whether investors incur economic costs when they observe a selected subset of market outcomes. Using data from Langton’s, Australia’s principal wine auction house, we apply a Markov Chain Monte Carlo model that jointly estimates latent prices and the probability of trading, correcting selection bias. Our auction setting offers direct observability of four outcomes – sold, passed-in, withdrawn, and never offered – making the selection mechanism transparent. We demonstrate that investors who ignore such selection effects create suboptimal mean-variance portfolios, forgoing 1.2% per month in certainty-equivalent returns, driven mainly by underestimated expected returns rather than misestimated covariances.

Title: Workers’ incentives and the optimal taxation of AI
Authors: Jakub Growiec, Klaus Prettner, Maciej Szkróbka
Abstract: We characterize the optimal tax policy in an economy with human manual and cognitive labor, physical capital, and artificial intelligence (AI). Extending the dynamic taxation setup of Slavík and Yazici (2014), we find that it is optimal to start taxing AI once cognitive workers find themselves at a disadvantage in the labor market relative to manual workers. This threshold may be crossed once AI becomes sufficiently capable in substituting humans across cognitive tasks.

Title: Editorial Board
How banking regulation affects collusion sustainability: A multimarket contact approach
Authors: Laura Prekwinkel, Duarte Brito, Helder Vasconcelos
Abstract: This paper investigates how regulatory instruments affect collusion sustainability in banking within a theoretical framework where: (i) banks compete simultaneously in loan and deposit markets characterized by different degrees of product differentiation; (ii) strategic interaction occurs through an infinitely repeated game with Nash reversion strategies; and (iii) capital requirements, reserve ratios, and interbank rates alter the relative profitability of each market. We show that the impact of these instruments on collusion depends critically on relative market differentiation: the same regulatory instrument can either facilitate or hinder coordination depending on which market exhibits greater product homogeneity. This non-monotonicity implies that regulators must account for market structure when calibrating policy instruments to avoid unintended effects on competitive intensity.

Title: Bootstrap inference for matching estimator under spatially correlated effects
Abstract: This paper proposes a dependent wild bootstrap (DWB) procedure for inference on matching estimators in the presence of spatial dependence. The bootstrap algorithm delivers a spatial heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent (HAC) variance estimator that accommodates unknown spatial dependence. By accounting for spatial correlation in the residuals, this approach improves the accuracy of standard error estimation for nonparametric matching estimators. A small Monte Carlo simulation illustrates its performance in a finite sample.

Title: Tipping into protectionism: Tariff shocks and the fragility of free trade
Abstract: This paper develops a dynamic political-economy model of trade-policy hysteresis. Tariffs reduce innovation and competitiveness but generate short-run benefits for import-competing sectors, creating incentives for myopic policymakers to adopt protectionism. The interaction between myopic protectionist policy and slow-moving competitiveness generates two stable steady states: a low-tariff, high-competitiveness regime and a high-tariff, low-competitiveness regime. Although free trade is welfare superior, it is politically fragile. Temporary tariff shocks that sufficiently erode competitiveness can permanently shift political incentives toward protectionism, trapping the economy in a low-competitiveness equilibrium with persistently high tariffs and lower welfare.

Title: A least-squares filter for sequence-space models
Abstract: This note introduces an algorithm for efficiently filtering unobserved shocks in linear sequence-space models. It solves a least-squares optimization problem in closed form that returns the expectation of a vector of unobserved shocks conditional on observed data. It handles heteroskedasticity, missing observations, measurement error, and non-Gaussian shock distributions. To illustrate its properties, I apply it to data simulated from a medium-scale heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian model and show that it accurately recovers the underlying structural shocks.

Title: Communication hierarchies with heterogeneous experts
Abstract: This paper studies a cheap talk game with two experts and a single receiver. The receiver may choose a communication hierarchy that determines the reporting order among experts. Experts are imperfectly informed and have different precisions in predicting the true state of the world. I show that with the introduction of heterogeneity in precisions, it may be optimal for the receiver to have a biased sender in their committee instead of an unbiased one, holding precisions constant. Thus, this paper shows how a standard result in cheap talk may be subverted with the introduction of heterogeneous experts.

Title: Elections and domestic violence
Authors: Anson Bouchard, Minjae Yun, Cameron A. Shelton
Abstract: Does post-election anger contribute to domestic violence? We study the 2020 US Presidential contest between Trump and Biden. Mapping block-level address data for domestic violence reports from as many of the 100 largest US cities as possible (20) to electoral precincts, we estimate diff-in-diff regressions to determine whether the pre-election vs. post-election difference in a precinct’s level of domestic violence is related to the precinct’s level of support for the losing candidate. We find that a 20-percentage point increase in the Trump two-party vote share correlates with an 8% increase in post-election domestic violence. Moreover, the effect is delayed until the recount was completed, suggesting that the effect observed is due to the resolution of the Presidential election rather than the act of voting, cessation of ads, or results of concurrent electoral contests.

Title: Humidity and work-related accidents
Authors: Nicolò Barbieri, Edoardo Santoni, Margherita Scarlato
Abstract: Analyzing almost 2.3 million work-related injuries in Italy, we estimate that higher humidity levels significantly increase the number of workplace accidents. Using dew point temperature to capture the moisture content of the atmosphere, our results confirm that a 1 °C increase in the dew point temperature raises the number of accidents by 0.7%. Allowing for non-linear effects of humidity, we uncover a U-shaped relationship highlighting that both low and high humidity levels are associated with a higher number of accidents relative to intermediate conditions.

Title: Are labor-controlled firms more innovative? Evidence from a regression discontinuity design
Abstract: We examine how labor representation on corporate boards affects innovation. Exploiting German co-determination law, which requires one-third (one-half) labor-elected directors in firms above 500 (2000) employees, we implement a regression discontinuity design using administrative employer-inventor-patent data. Crossing either threshold raises innovative productivity, measured as the forward citation-weighted number of patents per firm, by about 20%–25%. This increase is driven by more patents, while forward citations do not rise and decline significantly at the parity cutoff, indicating a shift toward more incremental, less path-breaking inventions. Additional evidence shows that labor-controlled firms insure workers against adverse labor market shocks, lengthen inventors’ employment spells, and offer wage incentives that reward patent quantity rather than quality. Overall, labor representation expands the number of patented inventions but dilutes their average citation impact, reallocating innovative effort in labor-controlled firms from path-breaking to incremental projects.

Title: Labor market effects of deleting delinquencies
Authors: Gonzalo Maturana, Jordan Nickerson, Santiago Truffa
